docs.title: Multi-Site Enterprise Network Lab
docs.text:
A home lab built in EVE-NG over the past year, while studying for CCNP ENCOR. Three sites, a shared core, an MPLS provider network, four Cisco operating systems, and an operations stack that monitors it, backs it up and controls who can log in, the way a real network would be run.

It was built around a full-time NOC support job, starting from no CCNA twelve months ago. There's a bit more on that further down, in case it's useful to anyone in the same position.

I'm publishing it for two reasons: to keep an open, checkable record of what I've built and what it taught me, and because most labs I found online stop at "configure the feature, screenshot it working, tear it down." This one stayed up, which meant living with the consequences of my own design decisions, including the bad ones. Several of those are documented below.

Don't take any of it on trust. The configs in this repo are the lab's real running configs with the secrets stripped out, and Verify it yourself gives the commands to check each claim. If something doesn't match, I'd like to know.

Want to build it yourself? Build it yourself walks through setting up EVE-NG on a Windows PC, adding the images, rebuilding the topology and loading the configs, and says which parts have no published config yet.

The lab in EVE-NG, October 2026. Both firewalls now sit inside Gret A, and the green block at the top is the MPLS provider network.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Scale About 45 EVE-NG nodes, 32 of them network devices under configuration backup, plus 14 routers being added for the next build Operating systems Cisco NX-OS, IOS-XE, IOS-XR, IOS Sites Gret A and Belv B (campuses), Site Q (branch), a shared core, and an MPLS provider network Separation 4 VRFs: CISCO-CORP, SCADA, PLc, DMZ Routing OSPF (multiple processes and areas, VRF-aware), MPLS L3VPN with BGP between the provider edge routers WAN Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN overlay, GRE-over-IPsec tunnels, MPLS L3VPN Multicast PIM sparse-mode, SSM, anycast rendezvous point with MSDP Security Palo Alto with GlobalProtect remote access, OPNsense with IPsec and WireGuard remote access, Cisco ISE, TACACS+, RADIUS with phone-based MFA Operations LibreNMS, Oxidized, Akvorado, FreeRADIUS, tac_plus, Ansible, custom health checks

docs.title: Plain-language translation
docs.text:
Networking carries a lot of jargon. Here's what the terms on this page mean without it, and where each one shows up in the lab.

Term In plain language Where it's used here VRF One physical box behaving as several separate routers. Traffic in one VRF can't reach another unless you deliberately join them. How the office, industrial and DMZ networks share hardware without sharing risk OSPF How routers tell each other which networks they can reach. "Areas" divide that up, so a change in one place doesn't make every router everywhere recalculate. Every site and the core BGP The routing protocol used between networks run by different people. It carries routes across organisations, with rules about which paths to prefer. Between the MPLS provider's edge routers, with much more of it in the next build MPLS L3VPN A provider network that carries several customers' traffic over the same routers while keeping each one private. PE routers sit at the provider's edge, P routers in its middle, and CE routers on the customer's side. The EIR-MPLS block SD-WAN Joining sites over any internet connection, with central controllers deciding how traffic should travel instead of each router being configured by hand. vManage, vSmart, vBond and an edge router at each site GRE over IPsec A tunnel that wraps traffic inside other traffic (GRE), then encrypts it (IPsec), so private networks can cross ones you don't trust. Between CORP-PBR-A and CORP-PBR-B Policy-based routing and IP SLA Sending traffic down a chosen path based on where it comes from, rather than whatever the routing table prefers. A probe (IP SLA) checks the path is alive and moves the traffic if it isn't. CORP-PBR-A and CORP-PBR-B QoS and shaping Deciding which traffic goes first when a link is busy. A shaper slows a link down on purpose, so the queuing has something to do and you can see it working. CORP-PBR-A Multicast Sending one copy of a stream that the network duplicates only where it's needed, rather than one copy per receiver. Used for video, market data and industrial telemetry. The rendezvous point is where senders and receivers find each other; anycast gives two routers the same address so either can do that job. All three sites TACACS+ and RADIUS Two ways of checking who may log into network equipment, and what they're allowed to type once they're in. Device logins, through Cisco ISE MFA with a one-time code Logging in takes the password and a six-digit code from a phone app, which changes every 30 seconds and can only be used once. Device logins SNMP How a monitoring system asks devices for their counters and health: traffic, errors, CPU, uptime. LibreNMS NetFlow Devices report a summary of every conversation crossing them (who talked to whom, and how much) to a collector. Metadata, not packet capture. Akvorado Configuration backup A system that logs into every device on a schedule, saves its configuration and keeps every version, so any change shows up as a before-and-after comparison. Oxidized, which is also where the configs in this repo come from RESTCONF and NETCONF Reading and changing a device's settings through an API, as structured data over HTTPS or SSH, instead of typing commands. CORP-PBR-A Control-plane policing Rate-limiting the traffic aimed at a device itself, such as logins and routing updates, so a flood can't overwhelm its processor. See Verify it yourself

Each campus has a Nexus switch at the boundary between site and core, holding the default gateways for the user networks. The two CORP-PBR routers exist because the virtual Nexus platform can't do policy-based routing or IPsec. They're a workaround, not a design choice.

Both firewalls now sit inside Gret A, behind NEXUS-A, so remote-access users arrive in a site rather than at the core. Cisco ISE and the operations server live there too. CE1 and CE2 connect the shared core to the MPLS provider network.

Management is a separate network per site with its own gateway. Every device sends SNMP, syslog, authentication and NetFlow from that network, keeping management traffic separable from user traffic.

docs.title: Routing and separation
docs.text:
Four VRFs are carried consistently from core to branch: CISCO-CORP for users, SCADA and PLc for isolated industrial networks, and DMZ for management and services. Each has its own OSPF process, so the four routing domains are genuinely independent rather than filtered versions of one.

The campus Nexus switches are area border routers: user networks in area 10 (Gret A) and area 20 (Belv B), core in area 0, with route summarisation and filtering at the boundary.

docs.title: MPLS L3VPN
docs.text:
A provider network built the way a real one is: six IOS routers in the middle (P routers) and two IOS-XR provider edge routers, PE1 and PE2, running OSPF and LDP between them, with BGP carrying the VPN routes from one edge to the other. Three of the four VRFs (SCADA, PLc and CISCO-CORP) cross it, each kept separate by its own route distinguisher. CE1 and CE2 connect the shared core to it.

It works, and it carries no traffic.

flowchart LR
    CE1[CE1] ---|"OSPF, per VRF"| PE1[PE1]
    PE1 ===|"MPLS labels + BGP VPN routes"| PE2[PE2]
    PE2 ---|"OSPF, per VRF"| CE2[CE2]
    CE1 -.-|"backdoor: the core's own OSPF links, preferred today"| CE2

The sites can already reach each other through the core's own OSPF links, and OSPF prefers a route it learns directly inside an area over the same route passed across a provider. That's the classic "backdoor" problem. The fix is either a sham-link or taking the backdoor away, and the next build does the second.

docs.title: Path control
docs.text: Policy-based routing on both CORP-PBR routers is designed to split traffic from two user networks across different core switches. On CORP-PBR-B that split isn't working yet (see below). Each path is watched by an IP SLA probe with a tracked object, so if a core switch stops responding the traffic moves. If every tracked path fails, the policy stands aside and lets normal routing take over rather than dropping traffic. That's worth knowing, because the alternative is a silent blackhole.

docs.title: WAN and encryption
docs.text:
A Catalyst SD-WAN overlay (vManage, vSmart, vBond and three edge routers), plus two GRE-over-IPsec tunnels between the CORP-PBR routers taking different physical paths through the two core switches. Both run OSPF inside the tunnel and have their MTU clamped, which avoids a well-known failure where small packets pass and large ones vanish.

vManage: the overlay's dashboard, and the controllers and edge routers it manages. Click any screenshot for the full-size version.

docs.title: Multicast
docs.text: PIM sparse-mode across all three sites, inside a VRF. Two routers share one rendezvous-point address (anycast), with MSDP peering between them so a source registering with one is visible to the other. Failover was tested by shutting the loopback on one and watching traffic continue. SSM and IGMPv3 are also configured.

docs.title: Quality of service
docs.text: Traffic is marked as it enters CORP-PBR-A. The queuing policy, and the shaper that creates artificial congestion so the queuing can actually be observed, are switched on for tests rather than left running. Without the shaper none of it does anything visible, which is the part most tutorials skip. The one time the shaper was left on, it throttled all inter-site traffic to 1 Mbps (more below).

docs.title: Security and access control
docs.text:
Palo Alto and OPNsense, as two different firewall platforms, deliberately. Cisco ISE is the policy engine for device logins across 26 devices, including per-command authorisation: a read-only account logs in successfully and is still refused configure terminal.

On top of that, multi-factor authentication: ISE passes the login to FreeRADIUS, which checks a rotating six-digit code from a phone authenticator app before allowing it.

sequenceDiagram

    participant Dev as Switch or router
    participant ISE as Cisco ISE
    participant FR as FreeRADIUS
    Eng->>Dev: Log in: password + code from phone app
    Dev->>ISE: TACACS+ request: is this login allowed?
    ISE->>FR: RADIUS request: check password and code
    FR-->>ISE: Accept, and record the code as used
    ISE-->>Dev: Accept, with this user's privilege level
    Eng->>Dev: configure terminal
    Dev->>ISE: TACACS+ request: may this user run this command?

ISE's TACACS+ live log: every login and command authorisation, per device and per user.

The two firewalls: Palo Alto PA-VM and OPNsense.

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text:
Both firewalls terminate remote-access VPNs from outside the lab. Palo Alto runs GlobalProtect. It was lost in the April rebuild and has been working again since October, reachable from the internet. OPNsense runs IKEv2 IPsec and WireGuard, used from a phone, giving access to the management networks.

Left: GlobalProtect connected, with traffic in both directions and an SSH session to NEXUS-A open. Right: the matching portal and gateway logs on the firewall. Public addresses are blurred.

OPNsense with an IKEv2 session up, and the phone end of both VPNs.

docs.title: Automation
docs.text: RESTCONF and NETCONF are enabled on IOS-XE and used to read the configuration and change it, such as setting interface descriptions over HTTPS rather than typing them at a CLI. YangSuite (in Docker) is there for exploring the data models. Ansible now pushes baseline settings to the IOS-XE devices from an inventory grouped by site and by platform, with first playbooks written for NX-OS and IOS-XR.

docs.title: LibreNMS: monitoring
docs.text:
SNMP polling across the estate: interface throughput and errors, device health, availability alerting. Setting it up properly meant working through polling-interval tuning, RRD step conversion, rrdcached, PHP timezone problems and SNMPv3 credentials. None of it is interesting until it's wrong, and all of it is part of running a monitoring platform.

LibreNMS: the overview dashboard and the device list.

docs.title: Oxidized: configuration backup
docs.text:
Every device's config pulled into a git repository on a schedule, so any change is a diff. That history is how I found several of the problems described on this page, and it's what keeps the published configs in this repo current. It's also the closest thing the lab has to a rollback mechanism.

It's here because I learned the hard way: when I moved the lab to a new machine in April, backups weren't fully working yet and most of it had to be rebuilt by hand (more below).

A config change shown as a diff, and the version history behind it.

docs.title: Akvorado: traffic analysis
docs.text:
NetFlow collection with a ClickHouse and Kafka pipeline behind it, fed by three exporters (both CORP-PBR routers and the branch edge). Networks are named per site, so flows read as gret-a-vlan20 → belv-b-vlan20 rather than raw addresses.

Getting flows to land took real debugging. First, NetFlow v9 templates expired while the collector restarted. Then a subtler one: every flow decoded perfectly and was then discarded, because the collector requires a sampling rate that unsampled IOS export never advertises. Found by reading the collector's own metrics, spotting an exact 1:1 ratio between decoded flows and sampling rate missing errors, and confirming it in the source.

docs.title: FreeRADIUS and tac_plus: authentication
docs.text: FreeRADIUS provides RADIUS and the one-time-code engine (PAM plus Google Authenticator). tac_plus is a standalone TACACS+ server built from source, kept as a fallback and as a plain reference implementation next to ISE's much larger one.

docs.title: lab-health.sh: custom health checking
docs.text:
A Bash script on a systemd timer, every fifteen minutes. Every check in it corresponds to something that actually went wrong:

  • Host basics: filesystem writable, disk space, clock synchronised (out-of-sync clocks silently break time-based one-time codes), resolver and Docker alive
  • Who owns the ports (2055, 49, 1812, 1813), because a leftover process squatting on the NetFlow port put the collector into a crash loop more than once
  • Container health, including a specific check for a container-DNS failure with the same effect
  • Functional tests, not just "is it running": a deliberately wrong RADIUS login that must be rejected; SNMP polls to each NetFlow exporter (which double as the collector's own prerequisite); a database freshness query broken down per exporter
  • Two specific settings that let logins keep working while quietly switching off the rule that stops a phone code being used twice. That's the dangerous kind of failure, because nothing looks wrong

It reports pass/fail, exits non-zero when something's broken, and with --fix repairs what's safe to repair automatically.

docs.title: What the ops stack taught me
docs.text: More than the network config did. Integrating five independent systems that were never tested together on one host is a large part of what infrastructure work involves. The failures were rarely exotic: port conflicts, systemd sandboxing making a directory read-only inside a service but not outside it, a PAM module trying to drop privileges to a user that didn't exist, and a monitoring script that gave different answers on identical runs because of a shell race between pipefail and grep -q.

docs.title: What I learned the hard way
docs.text:
Virtual platforms will lie to you. A switch port passed CDP (the neighbour appeared correctly) but forwarded no actual traffic. The switch even had an ARP entry for the far end, which turned out to have been learned from the far end's own broadcasts rather than from any reply. Moving the same virtual machine to a different switch fixed it instantly. When the control plane says yes and the data plane says nothing, bisect the path instead of re-reading the config.

Configuration can be valid and completely inert. Route summarisation configured for an area containing no interfaces. default-information originate in VRFs with no default route to originate. Both passed review. Neither did anything.

Filtering routes on a transit router can create a blackhole. Removing a route from one router's own table doesn't stop it advertising that path to everyone else, so neighbours keep sending traffic to a router that can no longer forward it. Reproduced deliberately and traced hop by hop, which taught me more than reading about it would have.

Overlapping addresses fail in confusing ways. Monitoring for both core switches kept failing. Two things were wrong at once: their management loopbacks overlapped the DMZ subnet, so ARP answers came from the wrong place, and one switch also had an SNMPv3 security-level mismatch. An address plan only protects you if something checks it for overlaps.

A network can work perfectly and carry nothing. Once the MPLS VPN was rebuilt on the right routers, the BGP session came up and 30 routes were exchanged, yet no traffic used it, because OSPF preferred the core's own links. "Working" and "in use" are different questions; check the path traffic actually takes, not just the routing table.

Old software and new tools don't always share a language. Older IOS images only offer SSH key-exchange methods that modern clients refuse. It broke Ansible on three routers and file transfers from vManage to an SD-WAN edge. When a connection fails before the password prompt, read the error before resetting any passwords.

Anything you expose gets found. Once the GlobalProtect portal was reachable from the internet, its logs filled with login attempts from scanners in several countries. They all failed at the client-certificate check, but "it's only a lab" stopped being true the moment it had a public address.

A security feature can switch itself off without anything looking wrong. A one-time code only works if the server records that it's been used, so nobody can use it again. Twice during the build that recording step silently failed: once because the software tried to switch to a user account that didn't exist, and once because the file it needed sat in a folder the service wasn't allowed to write to.

Both times, logins carried on working perfectly, with no error and nothing in the logs I was watching; codes had simply become reusable, which is the entire point of the feature. It's the failure I think about most, and the health checker now tests for both cases every fifteen minutes.

docs.title: What's wrong with it
docs.text:
The section I'd want to read if someone showed me this. The first version of this page listed eight problems; this is where each one stands now.

Problem in the first version Where it stands (October 2026) Over-engineered for its size Still true, and deliberate (see below) MPLS and BGP configured on the wrong routers Fixed. Rebuilt on the provider edge routers. It now works but carries no traffic (backdoor) Policy-based routing configured but never checked Half fixed. CORP-PBR-A now splits the two user networks; CORP-PBR-B still sends both down the same path A test shaper left throttling inter-site traffic to 1 Mbps Fixed. The shaper is no longer applied, but the habit behind it is still there (see below) Lab-grade credential handling Still true Everything runs on one server Still true Not reproducible Partly addressed. Ansible now pushes baseline settings, and a build guide covers rebuilding the lab by hand; most configuration is still typed by hand Backups have never been restored Still true

It's over-engineered for its size. Four VRFs, eight OSPF processes and three sites for around 30 devices is a feature-density decision, not an engineering one. A real network this size would be far simpler, and anyone proposing this design for 30 real devices should be challenged on it. It's a study environment, so the complexity is the point, but nobody should mistake it for good design at this scale.

Things still get configured and not verified. Policy-based routing was meant to split two user networks across different core switches. A config review found the primary and backup next-hops in the wrong order on both routers, so everything had quietly been using one path. CORP-PBR-A is fixed; the latest config from CORP-PBR-B still has both networks preferring the same next hop. Same lesson as the first time: I checked the configuration, not the behaviour.

Change discipline is thin. The 1 Mbps shaper went in for a test and was still there through three separate config reviews. It's gone now, but changes still go in with no record beyond Oxidized diffs, no pre-change checks and no test plan. In production that pattern causes outages.

Credential handling is lab-grade and would fail an audit. Several devices still keep a local account as a reversible type-7 password, and shared secrets are reused across services. Fine for a lab; genuinely bad if it were real. It's also why nothing here is published without going through a sanitiser first.

Everything runs on one server. LibreNMS, Oxidized, the NetFlow collector, RADIUS and TACACS+ all sit on a single Ubuntu box with no redundancy. If it dies I lose monitoring, backups, flow data and authentication at once. Losing authentication would lock me out of the devices too, if the local fallback accounts weren't there.

It's only partly reproducible. An Ansible inventory and baseline playbooks now push common settings, but most configuration is still typed or pasted by hand, with no single source of truth to rebuild from. April showed what that costs. The build guide lets someone rebuild most of the lab by hand, but it takes weeks of evenings, there's no lab export file, and the firewalls, ISE, the SD-WAN controllers and the MPLS provider routers have no published config. That's the biggest gap between this and how a modern network team works.

Backups have never been restored. Oxidized has been collecting configs for months. I have never once tested putting one back.

docs.title: The year behind it
docs.text:
Twelve months ago I didn't have a CCNA. I'm now preparing to sit CCNP ENCOR, and everything in this repository was built in the gaps around a full-time NOC support role.

There was no trick to it, but there was a lot of time. An hour or two on a normal weekday, before shifts or after them. And then the stretches that weren't normal: four, five, six hours a day across a whole weekend, disappearing into firewall configuration or standing OPNsense up from nothing. Some features went in over an evening. Some ate an entire weekend and were still broken on Sunday night.

In April I lost the lab. I moved from a 32GB laptop to a 128GB one, and because my configuration backups weren't fully working yet, most of it didn't come with me. I rebuilt it by hand. A working Palo Alto GlobalProtect VPN setup, which had taken a long fight to get going, didn't come back until October.

That's the honest origin of the operations stack on this page. Oxidized isn't here because a course told me to install it; it's here because I've already paid for not having it, and rebuilding thirty devices from memory is a lesson you only need once. The same goes for the health checker: it exists because things kept breaking silently, and I got tired of finding out days later.

Most of the time wasn't glamorous. A fair share went on things that turned out to be my own mistake, a virtual platform quietly not doing what it claimed, or a Linux service failing for reasons that had nothing to do with networking. The lessons and criticism sections above are mostly a record of that. I've left them in because the polished version would be less useful to anyone reading this, and less true.

If you're roughly where I was a year ago, four things helped more than anything else:

  • Keep one lab running instead of rebuilding it per topic. Consequences accumulate. Half of what I learned came from something I'd configured weeks earlier breaking when I touched something unrelated, and that's the part that actually resembles the job.
  • Break things deliberately, then predict the symptom before you look. Being able to recognise a failure is worth more than being able to configure the feature, and it's the harder half to pick up from a book.
  • Write it down as you go, and back it up sooner than you think you need to. The runbooks in this repo exist because I needed them, not because I planned to publish them. The backups exist because I learned the alternative in April.
  • Steady days get you there; the long ones move you forward. Most progress came from ordinary weekday hours. But the things I understand best are the ones I lost a weekend to, sitting with something broken long enough to actually work it out rather than reading the answer.

None of this required expensive kit or a lot of money: EVE-NG on a decent machine, free tooling, and time. It did require a genuine amount of that last one, and I'd rather say so than pretend it was effortless. If you're working in a NOC and wondering whether the jump to engineering-level work is realistic alongside shift work: it is. It's slow, it's occasionally demoralising, and it is absolutely possible.

└── scripts/           # publish script, sanitiser, health check, RESTCONF tools, Ansible playbooks, YangSuite

See Verify it yourself for commands you can run to check these claims rather than take them on trust, Build it yourself to set the lab up on your own PC, and the runbooks for the build notes behind each study phase.

Configurations are collected by Oxidized and published by a script that strips secrets and refuses to push if any survive. What's here reflects how the lab ran at the last sync, including whatever was broken at the time.

About AI help: I've used Claude, an AI assistant, throughout: as a study partner, for config reviews and for lab workbooks. Some of the scripts in scripts/ were written with its help. The lab was built and is run by me, and its configs are published here so the claims on this page can be checked.

docs.title: Build this lab yourself: EVE-NG on a Windows PC
docs.text:
This guide takes you from a Windows PC to a running copy of the lab: EVE-NG installed, images added, the topology rebuilt and the configs loaded. It points at the configs, screenshots and runbooks in this repo.

Last updated October 2026.

docs.title: 1. What you'll build, and what you need
docs.text:
The full lab is about 45 nodes: three sites, a shared core, an MPLS provider network, an SD-WAN overlay, two firewalls, ISE, and an Ubuntu operations server. Running all of it at once needs a host in the 128 GB RAM class. You don't need that to start: build it in stages and grow into it.

Before you begin, know four things:

  • No images are provided. Every Cisco and Palo Alto image here is licensed software, and you need your own (section 4).
  • There is no lab export file. You rebuild the topology by hand from the screenshot at docs/evidence/EVE-NG-Topology.png (section 5), then load the configs.
  • The published configs are sanitised. Every password, key and community has been replaced with a placeholder, and you put your own values in before they'll work (section 6).
  • Not every device has a published config. configs/ covers the campus, core and Site Q switches and routers, CE1 and CE2, and the three SD-WAN edge routers. PE1, PE2 and the P routers, the SD-WAN controllers, both firewalls, ISE and the WLC have none, so you build those from the vendors' guides and, for ISE, the AAA runbook.

The routers in enarsi/configs/ belong to the ENARSI build, which is still in progress. This guide doesn't cover them yet.

Hardware (approximate; check each vendor's sizing guide for the versions you use)

Build stage Host RAM CPU Disk Platform, core and campus (steps 1–2) 32 GB 8 threads with VT-x / AMD-V 200 GB SSD Adding WAN, SD-WAN and firewalls (steps 3–5) 64 GB 12+ threads 350 GB SSD Everything at once, including ISE 128 GB 16+ threads 500 GB SSD

ISE, vManage and the Nexus 9000v switches are the memory-hungry ones. You can run the lab in pieces: start only the nodes for the part you're working on.

What costs money

  • Free: EVE-NG Community Edition, VMware Workstation Pro (personal use), Ubuntu, OPNsense, and the whole ops stack (LibreNMS, Oxidized, Akvorado, FreeRADIUS, tac_plus).
  • Licensed: all Cisco images (IOL, IOSv, CSR1000v, Nexus 9000v, XRv, the SD-WAN controllers and edges, ISE, C9800-CL) and the Palo Alto PA-VM.

Suggested build order

  1. Platform: Windows prep, VMware, EVE-NG (sections 2–3)
  2. Core and campus: CSW1/2, NEXUS-A/B, distribution and access switches, the two PBR routers
  3. WAN: the MPLS PE/P routers, the CE routers, Site Q
  4. SD-WAN: vManage, vSmart, vBond and the three edges
  5. Security: Palo Alto, OPNsense, ISE, the WLC
  6. Operations: the Ubuntu server and its stack (section 9)

Expect a weekend for the platform and core. The full build is weeks of evenings.

docs.title: 2. Prepare the Windows PC
docs.text:
EVE-NG runs as a virtual machine inside VMware Workstation, and the devices run as VMs inside that. This nesting only works if the CPU's virtualisation extensions reach VMware directly: Intel VT-x/EPT or AMD's equivalent is a mandatory requirement. Source: EVE-NG

  1. Enable virtualisation in the BIOS/UEFI. Reboot into firmware setup and turn on Intel VT-x (Intel) or SVM / AMD-V (AMD). Without it, EVE-NG installs but nodes won't start.

  2. Turn off the Windows hypervisor. Windows features that use Hyper-V take the virtualisation extensions for themselves, and VMware can't nest. In an admin PowerShell:

    Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Hyper-V-All
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName VirtualMachinePlatform
Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName HypervisorPlatform
bcdedit /set hypervisorlaunchtype off

  3. Turn off Memory Integrity. Windows Security → Device security → Core isolation → Memory integrity: Off. This is virtualisation-based security, and it also holds the hypervisor.

  4. Reboot, then check. Run msinfo32. At the bottom of System Summary you want Virtualization Enabled in Firmware: Yes, and not A hypervisor has been detected. If that line is still there, something above is still on.
  5. Install VMware Workstation Pro. It's free with no licence key; you need a free Broadcom account to download it from the Broadcom Support Portal. Source: Broadcom EVE-NG supports Workstation 16.0 or later.
  6. Install the helper tools on Windows: WinSCP (to copy images onto EVE-NG), and PuTTY or the EVE-NG Windows client pack (so console links open in a terminal).

The trade-off: turning off Hyper-V also breaks WSL2, Docker Desktop and Windows Sandbox, which depend on it. If you use those, you'll be switching between the two setups with a reboot. A dedicated machine, or EVE-NG installed directly on hardware, avoids this and runs faster.

docs.title: 3. Install EVE-NG Community Edition
docs.text:
Download the free Community Edition, build a VM in Workstation with nested virtualisation ticked, and give it as much RAM as you can spare. EVE-NG's own step-by-step for VMware is section 3.1 of the EVE-NG Cookbook; this is the short version.

  1. Download the Community Edition ISO from the EVE-NG download page.
  2. Create the VM in Workstation: Custom → I will install the operating system later → Linux, Ubuntu 64-bit.
  3. CPU: as many cores as you can spare. Under Processors, tick Virtualize Intel VT-x/EPT or AMD-V/RVI. This one checkbox is what makes nested devices work.
  4. Memory: as much as possible, leaving about 8 GB for Windows. RAM is what limits how much of the lab runs at once.
  5. Disk: one virtual disk large enough for every image you'll add (see the table in section 1).
  6. Network adapter: NAT to start self-contained, or Bridged to put EVE-NG on your home LAN.
  7. Install: attach the ISO, boot, run the installer. On first boot EVE-NG asks for the root password, hostname and IP settings, and EVE-NG's first-boot guide walks through each prompt.
  8. Log in to the web UI at the IP shown on the console. Change the default admin password straight away.

  9. Update from the EVE-NG console in VMware Workstation: apt update && apt upgrade.

  10. Web UI loads from your Windows browser

  11. Default passwords changed (CLI and web)
  12. Images and nodes work: a node from any image you have starts and shows a console. That proves nesting works before you invest hours in images.

docs.title: 4. Get the images, upload and name them
docs.text:
Every Cisco and Palo Alto image here is licensed software, and the licence decides where you may run it. Free "image hub" sites redistribute these images without the vendors' permission, so this guide doesn't point to them.

CML images can't be used in EVE-NG. Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) includes nearly every Cisco image this lab uses, but Cisco licenses those images only for use inside CML: "Downloading these VM images and using them outside Cisco Modeling Labs without a proper license is prohibited." That covers IOL, IOL L2, IOSv and XRv, which Cisco distributes with CML. For the other Cisco images, EVE-NG needs downloads from Cisco Software Central under an entitlement, such as an employer's support contract.

No entitlement? Build the Cisco side in CML instead. CML's reference platforms cover IOL, IOSv, CSR1000v, Nexus 9000v, IOS XRv 9000, Catalyst SD-WAN, C9800-CL and ISE, and it ships FreeRADIUS and TACACS+ containers too. The topology, configs and runbooks here carry over; only the platform changes. Check your CML edition's node limit, because the full lab is about 45 nodes.

Image Lab nodes Get it from EVE-NG folder Disk file Cisco IOL L2 17.12 ASW/DSW-A and -B, the Q-SW switches Distributed with CML, for use in CML only /opt/unetlab/addons/iol/bin/ (a .bin file, no folder) none Cisco IOSv 15.9 Q-EDGE Distributed with CML, for use in CML only vios- virtioa.qcow2 Cisco CSR1000v 17.x CORP-PBR-A/B Cisco Software Central, with an entitlement csr1000vng- virtioa.qcow2 CSR1000v for SD-WAN Gret-Edge, Belv-Edge, Q-SDWANedge Cisco Software Central, with an entitlement csr1000vng- virtioa.qcow2 Cisco Nexus 9000v CSW1/2, NEXUS-A/B Cisco Software Central, with an entitlement nxosv9k- sataa.qcow2 Cisco XRv CE1/CE2, PE1/PE2 Distributed with CML, for use in CML only xrv- hda.qcow2 SD-WAN controllers vManage, vSmart, vBond Cisco Software Central, with an entitlement vtmgmt-, vtsmart-, vtbond- virtioa.qcow2 (vManage adds virtiob.qcow2) Cisco ISE 3.x ISE Cisco Software Central, with an entitlement ise- virtioa.qcow2 Cisco C9800-CL Gret-WLC Cisco Software Central, with an entitlement per the how-to per the how-to Palo Alto PA-VM PaloAlto Palo Alto customer support portal paloalto- virtioa.qcow2 OPNsense OPNsense-VPN opnsense.org, free per the how-to per the how-to Ubuntu 24.04 Server NOC-NMS-OPS ubuntu.com, free linux- virtioa.qcow2

Folder prefixes and disk names are from EVE-NG's naming table. After the prefix you add your own version label, e.g. nxosv9k-10.3.1. The EIR-MPLS P routers have no published config, so use any IOS or IOS-XR router image you have.

Upload each image

  1. Connect WinSCP to the EVE-NG IP as root.
  2. Create the folder, e.g. /opt/unetlab/addons/qemu/csr1000vng-17.3.8a/, and copy the disk in.

  3. Rename the disk to the name in the table. If the vendor ships a .vmdk, convert it on the EVE-NG console:

    qemu-img convert -f vmdk -O qcow2 image.vmdk virtioa.qcow2

  4. Fix permissions. EVE-NG won't see the image without this:

    /opt/unetlab/wrappers/unl_wrapper -a fixpermissions

  5. In a blank lab, add one node of that type and boot it before moving on to the next image.

docs.title: 5. Build the topology
docs.text:
There's no lab export file, so you recreate the topology by hand from the screenshot, one site at a time. It's the slowest step: about 45 nodes and their links. The screenshot is docs/evidence/EVE-NG-Topology.png, and the interface labels on every link are what you match.

  1. Create a new lab in EVE-NG and give it a name.
  2. Add nodes with the exact names from the screenshot: CSW1, NEXUS-A, CORP-PBR-A and so on. The configs, the Oxidized node list and the runbooks all refer to devices by those names.
  3. Set enough interfaces when you add each node. The Nexus switches use Ethernet1/x ports well above 1/8, and the IOL switches need extra port groups for e0/0–e3/3. Too few, and links have nowhere to land.
  4. Connect links port for port as labelled. The configs depend on the exact interfaces: a link on E1/5 instead of E1/6 leaves an IP address and an OSPF neighbour on a dead port.
  5. Build in the order from section 1: the core first, then the campus switches and PBR routers. Get OSPF neighbours up in the core before adding the next site, so problems stay small.
  6. Export the lab once it's built (More actions → Export). That file is your backup and your rebuild point.

Sites at a glance

Site Nodes Core CSW1, CSW2 (Nexus), CE1, CE2 (IOS XR) EIR-MPLS PE1, PE2 (IOS XR), and P routers EIR-MPLS-1–4, -A, -B Gret A Gret-Edge, NEXUS-A, CORP-PBR-A, DSW-A1/A2, ASW-A1–A3, Palo Alto, OPNsense, ISE, Gret-WLC, NOC-NMS-OPS Belv B Belv-Edge, NEXUS-B, CORP-PBR-B, DSW-B1/B2, ASW-B1–B3 Site Q Q-EDGE, Q-SDWANedge, Q-SW30–Q-SW34, Q-SW36 SD-WAN vManage, vSmart, vBond, a controller switch, an Internet router

docs.title: 6. Load the configs
docs.text:
The configs in configs/ are the real running configs with every secret replaced by a placeholder. Paste one as-is and the device rejects or mis-applies those lines, so replace each placeholder with your own value first.

What you'll find, and what to put there

Placeholder Was Replace with <REDACTED-KEY> TACACS+/RADIUS keys Your AAA shared secrets, matching the server side <SNMP-COMMUNITY> SNMP v2c community One read-only community, used everywhere <CERTIFICATE-REDACTED> Self-signed certificate blocks Delete the line; the device generates its own <REDACTED> Local passwords and secrets Your own admin and automation passwords <CONTACT> SNMP contact Any address, or delete the line <SNMP-V3-KEY> / <SNMP-V3-PASS> SNMPv3 auth and priv keys Cleartext passwords; NX-OS hashes them for you <TACACS-KEY> TACACS+ server key The same value as your tac_plus / ISE config <SERIAL> CSR1000v licence serial Delete the line; it's generated per VM <PSK> IPsec pre-shared keys One long random key, the same on both tunnel ends

Any other placeholder in angle brackets is a secret too and gets the same treatment. The domain name has also been rewritten to lab.internal, which works as-is.

Pick your values once, keep them in a file outside the repo, and reuse them. Several secrets have to match across devices: both ends of a tunnel, every switch and the RADIUS server. Making them up per device is how logins break.

Getting a config onto a node

  1. Boot the node and open its console from EVE-NG.
  2. Fill in the placeholders in a copy of that device's file (they're named by management IP, e.g. 10.99.0.1 = NEXUS-A).
  3. Paste in chunks of 20–30 lines rather than the whole file, because consoles drop characters on long pastes.
  4. Save it: write memory (IOS/IOS-XE), copy run start (NX-OS), commit (IOS-XR).
  5. Check: show ip interface brief and show ip ospf neighbor before moving to the next device.

The interface names in each config must match how you cabled the node in section 5. A mismatch is the most common reason a pasted config "doesn't work".

docs.title: 7. Connect the lab to your network
docs.text:
The lab reaches the outside world only through EVE-NG cloud networks, and how they meet your home network is yours to design. The author's home addressing and router setup aren't in this repo, and wouldn't fit your network anyway.

How clouds map: the Management (Cloud0) network is pnet0, bridged to the EVE-NG VM's first network adapter. Cloud1 to Cloud9 are pnet1–pnet9, bridged to the VM's second to tenth adapters. Add adapters in VMware to use them, and choose for each whether it's NAT, host-only or bridged to your LAN.

Cloud in the screenshot What it does here Safe default Management Out-of-band management for every device, and how the ops server reaches them Host-only or NAT, private to your PC Internet, SDWAN-Transit Internet path for the SD-WAN controllers and edges VMware NAT: outbound internet, nothing inbound HomeLAN The ops server's leg into a home network Leave unconnected unless you want the ops server reachable from your LAN GPoutside, WireGuard/IPsec VPN The firewalls' outside interfaces for remote-access VPN VMware NAT until you deliberately set up remote access (section 8)

Start with nothing bridged. Everything on host-only or NAT means nothing in the lab can be reached from your LAN or the internet. Add a bridge only when you have a reason for it.

Before you bridge anything, check two things:

  • Addressing overlap. The lab uses 10.x, 172.16.12.x and 192.168.x ranges. If your home LAN sits in one of them, re-address one side first, or routing breaks in confusing ways.
  • DHCP leaking. A lab device serving DHCP on a bridged network will hand addresses to your real devices. Check which lab interfaces run DHCP before bridging their segment.

docs.title: 8. Remote access and port forwarding: your router, your risk
docs.text:
This guide doesn't configure your home router, and nothing in the lab needs it to work. Remote access (reaching the lab from outside your home) is optional, and every port you forward is a door you've opened onto your home network. If you do it, you design it, and you own the result.

How this lab does it, as a pattern (not values to copy):

Service Forwarded port Lands on GlobalProtect remote-access VPN 443 TCP/UDP Palo Alto outside interface WireGuard 51820 UDP OPNsense IPsec (IKE, NAT-T) 500 and 4500 UDP OPNsense

Everything else (the EVE-NG web UI, LibreNMS, Oxidized, Akvorado, ISE, the firewall admin pages) is reached through a VPN, never forwarded directly.

If you set up your own:

  • Forward only VPN ports. Never forward a management web interface.
  • Require more than a password: certificate authentication, MFA, or both. A forwarded portal gets scanned within days. This lab's GlobalProtect logs show failed attempts from scanners in several countries, all stopped by the certificate requirement.
  • Keep PAN-OS and OPNsense patched. An exposed VPN on an old build is the standing risk.
  • Make the firewall rule between the lab and your home LAN deny-by-default, so a compromised lab VM can't reach your NAS, backups or personal machines.
  • Test from outside: from a phone on mobile data, run nmap -Pn -F <your WAN IP>. Anything open beyond the VPN ports you chose is a finding.
  • Don't be surprised by ports you didn't open. Some ISP routers answer on their own management ports (80, 443, 8080, 8443) from the WAN side. Those belong to the ISP's box, not your lab, and port forwarding can't close them.

If you publish your own build, keep your WAN IP, VPN keys, certificates and router screenshots out of it. Those are what turn a write-up into a map of your network.

docs.title: 9. The operations stack
docs.text:
The ops tools all run on one Ubuntu 24.04 Server node, NOC-NMS-OPS, on the management network. Install each tool from its own project documentation, then use the runbooks in docs/runbooks/ for the lab-specific wiring. The runbooks carry placeholders for secrets too, so use the same values you chose in section 6.

Tool Job Lab-specific guide in this repo LibreNMS SNMP monitoring and alerting Uses the SNMP community / v3 credentials from section 6 Oxidized Scheduled config backup into git Poll each device once, by management IP. Its config file holds the device login, so keep it outside any repo and chmod 600 it Akvorado NetFlow collection and analysis EVE-NG-SidePhase-Lab-Wide-Flows.md FreeRADIUS + Google Authenticator RADIUS with phone-based one-time passwords EVE-NG-SidePhase-AAA-TACACS-RADIUS-OTP.md tac_plus TACACS+, built from source Same AAA runbook, Part 0 scripts/lab-health.sh Health checks every 15 minutes Needs SNMP_COMMUNITY and RADIUS_LOCAL_SECRET set in its environment

The phase runbooks build the routing features in order once the topology is up:

  1. EVE-NG-Phase1-Filtering-PBR-Tunnel.md: OSPF filtering, policy-based routing with IP SLA, the second GRE/IPsec tunnel
  2. EVE-NG-Phase2-Multicast.md: PIM sparse-mode, SSM, anycast RP with MSDP
  3. EVE-NG-Phase3-Assurance-Automation.md: QoS, NetFlow, RESTCONF/NETCONF, AAA, control-plane policing

Publishing your own build? scripts/sanitize-configs.sh strips secrets from Oxidized exports and audits the result, and .gitleaks.toml adds the lab-specific secret rules gitleaks misses by default. Run both before anything goes public.

docs.title: 10. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Most failures come from four places: nesting, image naming, placeholders left in configs, and cabling that doesn't match the config.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Nodes start then stop at once; VMware says VT-x isn't supported Hyper-V or Memory Integrity still holds the hypervisor, or the VT-x box isn't ticked Redo section 2; msinfo32 must not say "A hypervisor has been detected" An image doesn't appear in the Add Node list Wrong folder prefix or disk file name, or permissions not fixed Check against the table in section 4, then run unl_wrapper -a fixpermissions Console is blank for a long time Some images boot slowly: Nexus 9000v, SD-WAN Manager and ISE take many minutes Wait, and watch the node's CPU in EVE-NG; ISE is the slowest by far Pasted config throws errors A placeholder wasn't replaced, or an interface name doesn't exist on that node Search the file for < before pasting; match interfaces to section 5 OSPF neighbours don't form Link on the wrong port, mismatched area, or MTU mismatch show ip ospf interface on both ends; compare against the screenshot's port labels RADIUS test times out instead of rejecting Service not running, or the client secret doesn't match Run freeradius -X in the foreground and watch the packet arrive Akvorado drops flows as "metadata missing" Its SNMP poll to the exporter's source address is failing Check the community and the device's SNMP ACL; the flows runbook explains the check SD-WAN edges won't join the controllers Certificates, organisation name or vBond reachability Follow EVE-NG's SD-WAN images how-to for the certificate setup Throughput is tiny on CSR1000v or PA-VM Unlicensed images run throttled or with limited features Expected in a lab; apply an evaluation licence if a test needs more Everything is sluggish More nodes running than RAM allows, so the host is swapping Stop nodes you're not using and run the lab in parts

docs.title: Verify It Yourself
docs.text:
Every claim in the overview, with the command that proves or disproves it. Don't take any of it on trust.

Two ways to use this:

  • With read-only access to the lab: run the commands in the Live sections. Everything here is read-only; nothing changes configuration.
  • With only this repository: the From the repo sections show how to check the same claims against the published configs using grep. Slower, but it works from a laptop with no access at all. Configs are saved under each device's management address, so CORP-PBR-A is configs/10.99.250.250 and NEXUS-A is configs/10.99.0.1.

If something doesn't match what's written, that's worth telling me about. Several of the problems listed in the overview's "what's wrong with it" section were found exactly this way.

docs.title: Getting in (if you have access)
docs.text:
ssh guest-ro@10.99.0.1        # NEXUS-A: campus switch, Gret A
ssh guest-ro@10.99.250.250    # CORP-PBR-A: core router, most of the interesting features
ssh guest-ro@10.99.2.1        # Q-EDGE: branch router

The account is read-only and enforced per command. Try configure terminal and you'll be refused. That refusal is itself one of the claims being tested, so it's a reasonable first thing to do.

docs.title: 1. "Four separate routing domains (VRFs)"
docs.text:
Claim: user, industrial and management traffic are in genuinely separate routing tables, not just filtered.

Live 

show vrf                                    ! NX-OS: lists CISCO-CORP, SCADA, PLc, DMZ
show ip route summary vrf CISCO-CORP
show ip route summary vrf SCADA

What proves it: each VRF has its own route count and its own prefixes. A route in SCADA does not appear in CISCO-CORP. That's separation at the routing-table level: the switch cannot forward between them even if it wanted to.

Quick disproof attempt: pick an address you can see in SCADA and look for it in the other table: 

show ip route 10.69.0.0 vrf CISCO-CORP      ! expect: not found

From the repo 

grep -c "^vrf context" configs/10.99.0.1                       # NEXUS-A
grep -A3 "^vrf context SCADA" configs/10.99.1.251              # CSW1

docs.title: 2. "OSPF with proper area design"
docs.text:
Claim: the campus switches are area border routers, summarising site networks into the core.

Live on NEXUS-A: 

show ip ospf vrf CISCO-CORP | include Area|border
show ip ospf neighbors vrf CISCO-CORP
show ip ospf database summary vrf CISCO-CORP

What proves it: the switch reports itself as an area border router, has neighbours in more than one area, and the summary database contains type-3 entries it generated. If it only had area 0 interfaces, none of that would be there.

From the repo 

grep -E "area 0.0.0.(10|20)" configs/10.99.0.1 configs/10.99.1.1   # NEXUS-A, NEXUS-B
grep -E "area .* range" configs/10.99.0.1                     # NEXUS-A

docs.title: 3. "Policy-based routing with automatic failover"
docs.text:
Claim: certain user traffic is forced down a chosen path, and moves automatically if that path fails.

Live on CORP-PBR-A: 

show ip policy                              ! which interface has the policy
show route-map PBR-POLICY                   ! the rules, and how many packets matched
show ip sla summary                         ! the probes watching each path
show track brief                            ! up/down state driving the failover

What proves it: the route-map shows a non-zero match count (traffic really is being policy-routed, not just configured), the SLA probes show OK, and the tracked objects show Up.

⚠️ This is one of the honest failures. The design was for two user networks to take different core switches. A review found the next-hops entered in the wrong order, so both were using the same one. Check whether it's been fixed:

show route-map PBR-POLICY | include next-hop

Sequence 10 and sequence 20 should prefer different first next-hops. If they both prefer the same one, the fix hasn't landed yet, and you've just verified a documented fault rather than a claim.

From the repo 

grep -A4 "route-map PBR-POLICY permit" configs/10.99.250.250   # CORP-PBR-A

docs.title: 4. "Multicast working across three sites"
docs.text:
Claim: PIM sparse-mode with two routers sharing one rendezvous-point address, linked by MSDP.

Live on CORP-PBR-A: 

show ip pim neighbor                        ! PIM adjacencies
show ip pim rp mapping                      ! the rendezvous point in use
show ip msdp summary                        ! peering with the other RP: state should be Up
show ip mroute                              ! actual multicast forwarding state

What proves it: show ip msdp summary in Up state means the two rendezvous points are exchanging source information. That's the mechanism that makes anycast RP work. show ip mroute showing (S,G) entries means real traffic is being forwarded, not just protocol state.

The interesting one: run show ip pim rp mapping on CORP-PBR-B too. Both routers claim the same RP address, 10.255.100.1. That's intentional: whichever is closer serves each device, and MSDP keeps them in sync.

From the repo 

grep -E "rp-address|msdp" configs/10.99.250.250 configs/10.99.250.251   # CORP-PBR-A, CORP-PBR-B

docs.title: 5. "Encrypted tunnels over two different paths"
docs.text:
Claim: two GRE-over-IPsec tunnels between the core routers, taking physically different routes.

Live 

show crypto session                         ! expect two sessions, different peers
show ip interface brief | include Tunnel
show ip ospf neighbors | include Tunnel
show interface Tunnel0 | include MTU

What proves it: two separate crypto sessions in UP-ACTIVE, both tunnels running a routing protocol inside them, and an MTU of 1400 rather than the default 1500. That last one is what stops large packets silently vanishing.

From the repo 

grep -A8 "^interface Tunnel" configs/10.99.250.250            # CORP-PBR-A

docs.title: 6. "Quality of service that actually does something"
docs.text:
Claim: traffic is marked, prioritised and queued, with counters to prove it.

Live on CORP-PBR-A: 

show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet1 input     ! marking
show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet2 output    ! queuing and shaping

What proves it: packet counters incrementing per class. A QoS policy with zero counters everywhere is configured but doing nothing, which is the normal state of most lab QoS.

⚠️ Another documented fault to check. A 1 Mbps shaper was applied for a test and left behind, rate-limiting all inter-site traffic. Look at the parent class:

show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet2 output | include shape|rate

If it shows a 1000000 target rate, the leftover is still there.

docs.title: 7. "Login requires a password and a phone code"
docs.text:
Claim: multi-factor authentication on network device logins.

Live: this one needs your own account rather than the guest one, so it's more of a demonstration than a self-service test. What you can verify independently:

show running-config | include tacacs|radius|aaa authentication

What proves it: the device points at both an ISE server and a RADIUS server, and every authentication list ends with local. That last word is the fallback that stops an authentication server outage locking everyone out permanently.

The bit worth understanding: the device itself knows nothing about one-time passwords. It sends the password to ISE, ISE forwards it to FreeRADIUS, and FreeRADIUS splits off the last six digits and checks them against the clock. No protocol changes anywhere, which is why this approach has worked since the 1990s.

From the repo 

grep -E "aaa authentication|aaa authorization" configs/10.99.2.39   # Q-SW39

Note every list ends in local. That's deliberate and it's the single most important habit in AAA rollouts.

docs.title: 8. "Per-command authorisation"
docs.text:
Claim: a read-only user can log in and still be denied configuration commands.

Live: the best test in this document, because you can run it on yourself:

show ip interface brief          ! works
ping 10.99.0.1                   ! works
configure terminal               ! "Command authorization failed"

What proves it: the login succeeded (you're at a prompt), but a specific command was refused. Authentication and authorisation are separate steps, and this is what the difference looks like in practice. Every command you type is checked against a server in real time.

docs.title: 9. "NetFlow is being collected"
docs.text:
Claim: three devices export traffic summaries to a collector.

Live 

show flow monitor FNF-MONITOR statistics     ! flows added, aged
show flow exporter FNF-EXPORTER statistics   ! packets actually sent
show flow monitor FNF-MONITOR cache format table | head -20

What proves it: the cache shows real conversations with byte and packet counts. Note that the monitor having flows and the exporter sending packets are two different things. A working cache with a zero export counter means the collector is receiving nothing, which is a failure mode I hit and didn't notice for a while.

docs.title: 10. "Control plane protection"
docs.text:
Claim: the branch router limits traffic to its own processor.

Live on Q-EDGE: 

show policy-map control-plane

What proves it: counters incrementing per class. Routing protocol traffic should be classified but not rate-limited (limiting it would break adjacencies); management traffic is limited.

Contrast worth seeing: the same idea on a Nexus, where it's on by default and can't be turned off: 

show copp status                             ! on CSW1

docs.title: Things you can safely break
docs.text:
If you have access and want to see the network react, these are reversible and won't damage anything. Ask first, as I may want to watch.

Test What to run What should happen Path failover Shut one core-facing interface while pinging between sites A few dropped packets, then recovery via the other core switch. show track brief flips to Down. Rendezvous point failover Shut Loopback100 on one PBR router Multicast keeps flowing. The other router's copy of the anycast address takes over. Authentication fallback Stop the RADIUS service The one-time-password account fails; the local account still works after a short pause. This is why local is on every list. Replay protection Log in with a one-time code, then immediately reuse the same code Rejected. Codes are single-use, and this check silently stopped working twice during the build, which is why it's now monitored.

docs.title: If you find something wrong
docs.text: Genuinely, please say. The configs are published from the live devices, so what's here is what was running at the last sync, including anything broken at the time. Two of the faults documented in the overview were found by re-reading my own configs weeks later, and I'd rather know about the third.

docs.title: Phase 1 — OSPF Filtering, PBR + IP SLA, Second GRE/IPsec Tunnel
docs.text:
Three tasks, one evening each, zero new nodes. Covers the checklist lines: OSPF filtering (four methods, including the LSDB-vs-RIB distinction), conditional debug, PBR (upgraded with tracking), IP SLA, and GRE tunnelling + IPsec (second tunnel, plus reading crypto failures).

Order doesn't depend on Phase 2 — run these in either sequence. All object names below (PBR-POLICY, PBR-ACL20/40, GRE-TS, GRE-IPSEC-PROFILE) are your existing ones, verified from the current export.

Prerequisite (skip if you did Phase 2 Part 0): the NEXUS-A dead sub-if deletions — 

! NEXUS-A
no interface Ethernet1/6.30
no interface Ethernet1/7.30

docs.title: Task 1 — OSPF filtering on your real ABRs
docs.text: You built genuine ABRs when the user SVIs moved to area 0.0.0.10. Site A's prefixes (10.1.0.0/24, 10.2.0.0/24, 10.4.0.0/24, 10.98.0.0/24) enter the backbone as Type-3 summaries generated by NEXUS-A. That boundary is where three of the four filtering methods live.

docs.title: 1.0 Baseline — know what you're about to remove
docs.text:
! PBR-B
show ip route 10.4.0.0 255.255.255.0        ! O IA, learned from area 0
show ip ospf database summary | i 10.4.0.0  ! the Type-3, advertised by 1.1.1.1 (NEXUS-A)

Expect both present. Every method below makes one or both disappear — the which is the lesson.

docs.title: 1.1 Method 1 — area filter-list at the ABR
docs.text:
Blocks the Type-3 from ever being generated into area 0. NX-OS flavour uses a route-map (IOS uses a prefix-list directly — know both for the exam).

! NEXUS-A
ip prefix-list PL-AREA10-OUT seq 5 deny 10.4.0.0/24
ip prefix-list PL-AREA10-OUT seq 10 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32
!
route-map RM-AREA10-OUT permit 10
  match ip address prefix-list PL-AREA10-OUT
!
router ospf 1
  vrf CISCO-CORP
    area 0.0.0.10 filter-list route-map RM-AREA10-OUT out

IOS equivalent for your notes: router ospf 1 → area 10 filter-list prefix PL-AREA10-OUT out

Verify on PBR-B: route gone and LSA gone — show ip ospf database summary | i 10.4.0.0 returns nothing. The ABR never created it, so nobody in area 0 has it. Site-A VLAN40 is now unreachable inter-site (flows die at whichever hop runs out of route — note that PBR shifts the drop point but can't save a flow nobody can route).

Remove before the next method: 

router ospf 1
  vrf CISCO-CORP
    no area 0.0.0.10 filter-list route-map RM-AREA10-OUT out
Confirm 10.4.0.0/24 returns on PBR-B.

docs.title: 1.2 Method 2 — range … not-advertise (summarisation as a filter)
docs.text:
Same observable, different mechanism: the range that creates the summary is told not to advertise it. You already have the range line — just re-enter it with the keyword:

! NEXUS-A
router ospf 1
  vrf CISCO-CORP
    area 0.0.0.10 range 10.4.0.0/24 not-advertise

Verify identical disappearance on PBR-B, then restore: 

    area 0.0.0.10 range 10.4.0.0/24

Exam framing: method 1 is a filter applied at the boundary; method 2 is the summarisation machinery itself suppressing. Same result here because your ranges are 1:1 — with real aggregation they behave differently (a range hides components; a filter-list can kill the aggregate).

docs.title: 1.3 Method 3 — distribute-list in (the LSDB-vs-RIB demonstration)
docs.text:
The one the guide warns about, experienced. This filters RIB installation only — the LSA stays, the flooding continues, downstream routers still compute paths through you.

Deliberately using 10.1.0.0/24 (Vlan10, site A) here, not 10.2.0.0/24 — reason at the end.

! PBR-B
ip prefix-list PL-RIB-DENY seq 5 deny 10.1.0.0/24
ip prefix-list PL-RIB-DENY seq 10 permit 0.0.0.0/0 le 32
!
router ospf 1
 distribute-list prefix PL-RIB-DENY in

Now read the three truths: 

! PBR-B — route gone from RIB:
show ip route 10.1.0.0 255.255.255.0          ! % Network not in table

! PBR-B — but the LSA is still right there:
show ip ospf database summary | i 10.1.0.0    ! present, untouched

! NEXUS-B — still trusts PBR-B completely:
show ip route 10.1.0.0/24 vrf CISCO-CORP      ! installed, next-hop 10.10.71.2 (PBR-B!)

Prove the blackhole: 

! NEXUS-B
ping 10.1.0.1 vrf CISCO-CORP source 10.1.1.1   ! dies - AT PBR-B

NEXUS-B forwards to PBR-B because the LSDB says so; PBR-B has no route and drops. That's why distribute-list in is dangerous on a link-state transit router — you filtered your own RIB but kept advertising competence you no longer have.

Why not 10.2.0.0/24? Try it after, if curious: flows from 10.2.1.0/24 to 10.2.0.0/24 match PBR-ACL20 on Gi1, and PBR is consulted before the RIB — the policy forces next-hop 10.20.30.1 and the traffic sails straight over the hole. PBR masking a missing route is a great thing to have seen once (and a preview of Task 2's theme).

Cleanup: 

router ospf 1
 no distribute-list prefix PL-RIB-DENY in
no ip prefix-list PL-RIB-DENY

docs.title: 1.4 Method 4 — filtering at redistribution (ASBR)
docs.text:
The guide's example, run for real. PBR-A becomes an ASBR:

! CORP-PBR-A
ip route 192.168.100.0 255.255.255.0 Null0
ip prefix-list REDIST-STATIC seq 5 permit 192.168.100.0/24
route-map STATIC-TO-OSPF permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list REDIST-STATIC
!
router ospf 1
 redistribute static subnets route-map STATIC-TO-OSPF

Verify it floods domain-wide as external: 

show ip route ospf | i 192.168.100           ! on PBR-B: O E2
show ip route 192.168.100.0/24 vrf CISCO-CORP ! on CSW1: same
show ip ospf | i boundary                    ! PBR-A now reports ASBR

Now tighten the filter and watch the Type-5 get flushed: 

no ip prefix-list REDIST-STATIC seq 5 permit 192.168.100.0/24
ip prefix-list REDIST-STATIC seq 5 deny 192.168.100.0/24
The E2 vanishes everywhere within seconds. Cleanup: remove the redistribute line, the static, the prefix-list and route-map.

docs.title: 1.5 Conditional debug — capture a full adjacency FSM
docs.text:
PBR-A has multiple OSPF neighbors; the condition keeps the noise down to one interface — that's the entire point of the technique.

! CORP-PBR-A
debug condition interface GigabitEthernet1
debug ip ospf adj
show debug condition          ! confirm the gate is set

Bounce the far end: 

! NEXUS-A
interface Ethernet1/8
  shutdown
  no shutdown

Expected on PBR-A: only the Gi1 neighbor's events — DOWN, then INIT → EXSTART → EXCHANGE → LOADING → FULL (2-WAY flashes past on point-to-point). Write down which state does what; it's a favourite exam sequence. Then, always, in this order:

undebug all
no debug condition all

NX-OS side of the same story, no debug needed: show ip ospf internal event-history adjacency on NEXUS-A — the always-on flight recorder is the NX-OS answer to conditional debugging.

docs.title: 1.6 Stub/NSSA — why it's parked
docs.text: Area 0.0.0.10 contains no routers other than the ABR itself (the DSWs are L2), so converting it to stub changes nothing observable — there's nobody inside to receive the injected default. It'll be a proper exercise in the 3-router pod (Phase 4).

docs.title: Task 2 — PBR grows reflexes: IP SLA + verify-availability
docs.text: Current behaviour: PBR-POLICY seq 10 forces VLAN20-sourced inter-site traffic to CSW1 (10.10.30.1), seq 20 forces VLAN40 to CSW2 (10.10.60.1), seq 30 lets everything else route normally. If a next-hop dies, plain set ip next-hop only gives up when the interface goes down. Tracking makes each class fail over to the other core switch deliberately.

docs.title: 2.1 Probes and tracks
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-A
ip sla 10
 icmp-echo 10.10.30.1 source-interface GigabitEthernet2
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 10 life forever start-time now
ip sla 20
 icmp-echo 10.10.60.1 source-interface GigabitEthernet3
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 20 life forever start-time now
!
track 10 ip sla 10 reachability
track 20 ip sla 20 reachability

! CORP-PBR-B — mirror
ip sla 10
 icmp-echo 10.20.30.1 source-interface GigabitEthernet2
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 10 life forever start-time now
ip sla 20
 icmp-echo 10.20.60.1 source-interface GigabitEthernet3
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 20 life forever start-time now
!
track 10 ip sla 10 reachability
track 20 ip sla 20 reachability

Confirm before touching the route-map: show track brief → both Up; show ip sla statistics | i Latest → return codes OK.

docs.title: 2.2 Swap the set clauses
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-A
route-map PBR-POLICY permit 10
 no set ip next-hop 10.10.30.1
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.10.30.1 1 track 10
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.10.60.1 2 track 20
route-map PBR-POLICY permit 20
 no set ip next-hop 10.10.60.1
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.10.60.1 1 track 20
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.10.30.1 2 track 10

! CORP-PBR-B
route-map PBR-POLICY permit 10
 no set ip next-hop 10.20.30.1
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.20.30.1 1 track 10
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.20.60.1 2 track 20
route-map PBR-POLICY permit 20
 no set ip next-hop 10.20.60.1
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.20.60.1 1 track 20
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.20.30.1 2 track 10

Each class: primary next-hop gated by its track, backup gated by the other. Sequence numbers (1, 2) are the preference order.

docs.title: 2.3 Prove normal operation
docs.text:
Test traffic that matches the ACLs — source the pings from the site SVIs:

! NEXUS-A
ping 10.2.1.1 vrf CISCO-CORP source 10.2.0.1    ! matches PBR-ACL20 -> via CSW1
ping 10.2.1.1 vrf CISCO-CORP source 10.4.0.1    ! matches PBR-ACL40 -> via CSW2


! CORP-PBR-A
show route-map PBR-POLICY        ! match counters on seq 10 / seq 20 incrementing
show ip policy                   ! Gi1 -> PBR-POLICY
debug condition interface GigabitEthernet1
debug ip policy                  ! per-packet: "policy match" + "FIB policy route" lines
(undebug all / no debug condition all when done — it's per-packet.)

docs.title: 2.4 Break 1 — real failover
docs.text:
Start a long ping from NEXUS-A (ping 10.2.1.1 vrf CISCO-CORP source 10.2.0.1 count 500), then:

! CSW1
interface Ethernet1/5
  shutdown

Expected: a few drops while the probe times out (frequency 5s — a couple of cycles), then the stream continues. show track brief → track 10 Down, 20 Up. debug ip policy now shows the VLAN20 class using 10.10.60.1 — same policy, second next-hop. no shutdown, watch track 10 return.

docs.title: 2.5 Break 2 — everything down, and PBR fails open
docs.text:
No topology damage needed — point both probes somewhere unrouted (an SLA op must be deleted to change its target):

! CORP-PBR-A
no ip sla 10
ip sla 10
 icmp-echo 192.0.2.1 source-interface GigabitEthernet2
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 10 life forever start-time now
no ip sla 20
ip sla 20
 icmp-echo 192.0.2.1 source-interface GigabitEthernet3
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 20 life forever start-time now

Both tracks go Down — and the pings from NEXUS-A keep working. debug ip policy shows the tell: policy rejected -- normal forwarding. With every verified next-hop dead, PBR steps aside and the routing table carries the traffic. That's the behaviour the exam (and change reviews) ask about: tracked PBR degrades to normal routing, it doesn't blackhole.

Restore both SLAs to their real targets (10.10.30.1 / 10.10.60.1) the same delete-and-recreate way.

docs.title: Task 3 — the second GRE/IPsec tunnel (…60 path)
docs.text: You pre-provisioned this without noticing: both PBRs already carry network 172.16.12.4 0.0.0.3 area 0, and the isakmp keys for the Gi3-side peers are in place (and correctly spelled, now). The OSPF adjacency will form the moment the tunnel exists — which makes it the perfect conditional-debug subject.

docs.title: 3.1 Arm the debug first
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-A
debug condition interface Tunnel1
debug ip ospf adj

docs.title: 3.2 Build both ends
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-A
interface Tunnel1
 description GREto-PBR-B-via-60path
 ip address 172.16.12.5 255.255.255.252
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet3
 tunnel destination 10.20.60.2
 tunnel protection ipsec profile GRE-IPSEC-PROFILE

! CORP-PBR-B
interface Tunnel1
 description GREto-PBR-A-via-60path
 ip address 172.16.12.6 255.255.255.252
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet3
 tunnel destination 10.10.60.2
 tunnel protection ipsec profile GRE-IPSEC-PROFILE

(tunnel mode gre ip is the default; sharing GRE-IPSEC-PROFILE across both tunnels is fine — each source/destination pair negotiates its own SAs.)

Expected on PBR-A's debug: IKE completes, Tunnel1 comes up, and the OSPF FSM scrolls past for the new neighbor only — the pre-existing network 172.16.12.4 statement catches it with zero further config. undebug all / no debug condition all.

docs.title: 3.3 Verify the pair
docs.text:
show ip ospf neighbor                       ! new FULL neighbor on Tunnel1
show crypto session                         ! TWO sessions: peers 10.20.30.2 and 10.20.60.2
show crypto isakmp sa                       ! both QM_IDLE
show crypto ipsec sa | i peer|encaps|decaps ! counters on both peers
show ip ospf interface Tunnel1 | i Cost     ! ~1000 (default 100 kbps tunnel bandwidth)

That cost is why neither tunnel attracts transit traffic — physical paths cost single digits. The tunnels are overlay-in-waiting, exactly as designed.

While you're here, Tunnel0 on both ends is missing the MTU/MSS hardening — add it: 

interface Tunnel0
 ip mtu 1400
 ip tcp adjust-mss 1360
(GRE adds 24 bytes, the IPsec transform another ~56 — without these, full-size TCP through the tunnel fragments or blackholes on PMTUD-hostile paths. A classic real-world GRE/IPsec gotcha.)

docs.title: 3.4 Break — phase-2 mismatch, and the diagnostic that names it
docs.text:
On one side only, wrap Tunnel1 in a deliberately wrong transform:

! CORP-PBR-B
crypto ipsec transform-set TS-WRONG esp-aes esp-sha256-hmac
 mode tunnel
crypto ipsec profile PROF-WRONG
 set transform-set TS-WRONG
!
interface Tunnel1
 tunnel protection ipsec profile PROF-WRONG

(Your live set is esp-aes 256 esp-sha-hmac; TS-WRONG differs in both cipher strength and hash, so the phase-2 proposal can't match.)

Read the failure signature: 

show crypto isakmp sa                        ! peer 10.10.60.2 STILL QM_IDLE - phase 1 is fine
show crypto ipsec sa peer 10.10.60.2         ! no SAs / zero counters
show crypto session                          ! that peer: DOWN-NEGOTIATING
show interface Tunnel1 | i line protocol     ! down (protection configured, no SA)

ISAKMP up + IPsec down = phase-2 problem (transform or proxy mismatch). Compare with the phase-1 signature you've already lived through in this lab: a PSK mismatch never reaches QM_IDLE — it thrashes in MM_NO_STATE. You ran that experiment involuntarily with a mistyped key; now you know both failure faces on sight.

Restore: 

! CORP-PBR-B
interface Tunnel1
 tunnel protection ipsec profile GRE-IPSEC-PROFILE
no crypto ipsec profile PROF-WRONG
no crypto ipsec transform-set TS-WRONG esp-aes esp-sha256-hmac

If you ran Phase 2 already and left PIM on Tunnel0, one line (ip pim sparse-mode) on each Tunnel1 keeps the tunnels symmetric.

docs.title: Rollback (complete)
docs.text: Task 1 cleans up as it goes — nothing persists except knowledge. Task 2: to revert to untracked PBR: re-enter plain set ip next-hop <primary> under each sequence, no set ip next-hop verify-availability … for both entries, then no track 10/20, no ip sla 10/20 (per PBR). Task 3: no interface Tunnel1 both ends (the network 172.16.12.4 statement can stay, as it did before); MTU/MSS lines on Tunnel0 are keepers.

docs.title: Checklist mapping
docs.text: ENCOR line Where you did it OSPF filtering — area filter-list 1.1 (NX-OS route-map flavour + IOS syntax noted) OSPF filtering — summarisation/not-advertise 1.2 OSPF filtering — distribute-list in / LSDB vs RIB 1.3 (with the transit blackhole proven) OSPF filtering — redistribution route-map 1.4 Conditional debug 1.5, 2.3, 3.1 (three different uses) PBR Task 2 (verify-availability, fail-over, fail-open) IP SLA Task 2 probes + tracks GRE tunnelling + IPsec Task 3 (build, MTU/MSS, phase-1 vs phase-2 failure signatures)

docs.title: Phase 2 — Multicast Across the CORP VRF
docs.text:
Covers the whole multicast line of your checklist: PIM-SM, IGMPv2, IGMPv3, SSM, MSDP (as anycast-RP), plus BiDir at describe-level and RPF manipulation with static mroutes. Everything runs on existing devices — no new nodes.

Time budget: Parts A–D one evening. Part E ~45 min. Parts F–G another hour.

docs.title: The multicast domain
docs.text:
SOURCE                                                        RECEIVER
 NEXUS-A Vlan10 (10.1.0.1/24, area 10)          NEXUS-B Vlan10 (10.1.1.1/24, area 10)
        |                                                          |
      E1/8 ──── Gi1  PBR-A  Gi2 ──── E1/5 CSW1 E1/6 ──── Gi2  PBR-B  Gi1 ──── E1/8
                 |  (RP: Lo100)                                |
                 Gi3 ─────── E1/5 CSW2 E1/6 ─────────────────── Gi3
                 |                                             |
                 └──────────── Tunnel0 (172.16.12.0/30) ────────┘   (in OSPF, high cost)

All in VRF CISCO-CORP on the NX-OS boxes, global table on the PBR CSRs (they're the same OSPF domain).

Address plan (verified unused in the lab):

Item Value ASM group 239.1.1.10 SSM group 232.1.1.1 BiDir group range 239.200.1.0/24 RP (later anycast) 10.255.100.1/32 = PBR-A Loopback100 (Part F adds the same on PBR-B) MSDP peer IDs PBR-A Lo101 = 10.255.101.1/32, PBR-B Lo101 = 10.255.101.2/32

RPF prediction worth knowing up front: PBR-B has two equal-cost paths toward site A (via CSW1 next-hop 10.20.30.1, via CSW2 next-hop 10.20.60.1). With ECMP, IOS RPF picks the highest next-hop IP → expect the tree to pin through CSW2. You'll verify and then break this in Part E.

docs.title: Part 0 — prerequisite
docs.text:
Apply the outstanding NEXUS-A fix first, or RPF toward PBR-A's Gi2/Gi3 subnets is ambiguous and this lab will behave randomly:

! NEXUS-A
no interface Ethernet1/6.30
no interface Ethernet1/7.30

Confirm before continuing: show ip route 10.10.30.2 vrf CISCO-CORP on CSW1 shows a single path via E1/5.

docs.title: CORP-PBR-A (IOS-XE)
docs.text:
ip multicast-routing distributed
!
interface Loopback100
 description RP-ANYCAST
 ip address 10.255.100.1 255.255.255.255
 ip pim sparse-mode
!
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip pim sparse-mode
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip pim sparse-mode
interface GigabitEthernet3
 ip pim sparse-mode
!
router ospf 1
 network 10.255.100.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
!
ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1

docs.title: CORP-PBR-B (IOS-XE)
docs.text:
ip multicast-routing distributed
!
interface GigabitEthernet1

interface GigabitEthernet2

interface GigabitEthernet3

!
ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1

docs.text:
feature pim
!
interface Ethernet1/5
  ip pim sparse-mode
interface Ethernet1/6
  ip pim sparse-mode

vrf context CISCO-CORP

docs.text:

!
interface Ethernet1/8

interface Vlan10
  ip pim sparse-mode

vrf context CISCO-CORP

docs.title: NEXUS-B (NX-OS)
docs.text:

!
interface Ethernet1/8
  ip pim sparse-mode
interface Vlan10

vrf context CISCO-CORP
