docs.title: Verify Part A (do this before Part B)
docs.text:
! IOS-XE
show ip pim neighbor          ! PBR-A expects 3 (Gi1/Gi2/Gi3); PBR-B expects 3
show ip pim rp mapping        ! Static: 10.255.100.1 for 224.0.0.0/4
show ip pim interface

! NX-OS
show ip pim neighbor vrf CISCO-CORP    ! CSWs expect 2; NEXUS boxes expect 1 (E1/8)
show ip pim rp vrf CISCO-CORP
show ip pim interface vrf CISCO-CORP brief

Nothing forwards yet — that's correct. PIM-SM is pull-based: no receivers, no tree.

docs.title: Part B — first stream (IGMPv2, Register, SPT)
docs.text: Receiver goes on PBR-B Gi1 first because IOS-XE reliably answers pings to joined groups — a clean success gate before you involve NX-OS punting quirks.

docs.title: 1. Join the receiver — CORP-PBR-B
docs.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip igmp join-group 239.1.1.10

Immediately check the shared tree built toward the RP: 

show ip mroute 239.1.1.10              ! on PBR-B: (*,G), RP 10.255.100.1, flags SJCL, OIF Gi1
show ip mroute vrf CISCO-CORP 239.1.1.10   ! on CSW2: (*,G) IIF E1/5, OIF E1/6
show ip mroute 239.1.1.10              ! on PBR-A (RP): (*,G) with OIF toward CSW2 (Gi3)
If CSW1 has the (*,G) instead of CSW2, your ECMP tiebreak landed differently — fine, just note which core switch owns the tree and mirror the Part E break accordingly.

docs.title: 2. Watch registration happen — on PBR-A
docs.text:
debug condition interface GigabitEthernet1
debug ip pim 239.1.1.10
(Conditional debug from your checklist, applied for real: the Register arrives as unicast from NEXUS-A via Gi1.)

docs.title: 3. Start the source — NEXUS-A
docs.text:
ping multicast 239.1.1.10 interface vlan 10 count 100
(If your NX-OS build rejects that syntax, try ping 239.1.1.10 interface vlan 10 count 100.)

Expected: replies from 10.10.71.2 (PBR-B's Gi1 — multicast pings are answered unicast by each joined responder). On PBR-A's debug: Received v2 Register then Send v2 Register-Stop — the FHR-to-RP handshake, once. Then undebug all.

docs.title: 4. Read the steady-state tree
docs.text:
! PBR-B
show ip mroute 239.1.1.10       ! now ALSO an (S,G): (10.1.0.1, 239.1.1.10), flags include T = SPT
show ip rpf 10.1.0.1            ! RPF neighbor 10.20.60.1 via Gi3 (the CSW2 prediction)
show ip mroute count            ! forwarded counters incrementing

! NX-OS hops
show ip mroute vrf CISCO-CORP detail   ! per-entry packet stats
The *(,G) → Register → Register-Stop → (S,G)/SPT sequence you just watched is the entire PIM-SM exam narrative in one ping.

docs.title: Part C — receiver on a real LAN SVI (NX-OS IGMP)
docs.text: Now move the receiver where it belongs — site B's user VLAN:

docs.title: NEXUS-B
docs.text:
interface Vlan10
  ip igmp join-group 239.1.1.10

Re-run the source ping from NEXUS-A. Verify: 

show ip igmp groups vrf CISCO-CORP          ! 239.1.1.10 on Vlan10, v2
show ip mroute vrf CISCO-CORP 239.1.1.10    ! on NEXUS-B: OIF Vlan10, IIF E1/8

Two NX-OS realities worth knowing (both exam-adjacent): - join-group punts the traffic to the supervisor. N9Kv may or may not answer the pings — the mroute counters are your proof of forwarding, replies are a bonus. - The production-grade alternative is ip igmp static-oif 239.1.1.10 — adds the OIF without punting, switch won't reply at all. Swap it in and observe the difference if you like.

Optionally remove the PBR-B join now to keep state clean: 

interface GigabitEthernet1
 no ip igmp join-group 239.1.1.10

docs.title: Part D — SSM with IGMPv3
docs.text: Platform asymmetry to notice: NX-OS enables the 232.0.0.0/8 SSM range by default the moment PIM is on; IOS-XE needs it switched on.

docs.title: CORP-PBR-A and CORP-PBR-B
docs.text: ip pim ssm default

docs.title: Receiver — NEXUS-B (IGMPv3 join with the source specified)
docs.text:
interface Vlan10
  ip igmp version 3
  ip igmp join-group 232.1.1.1 source 10.1.0.1

docs.title: Source — NEXUS-A
docs.text: ping multicast 232.1.1.1 interface vlan 10 count 100

docs.title: Verify — the SSM signature
docs.text:
show ip mroute 232.1.1.1                     ! IOS: (S,G) ONLY - no (*,G), flags include s
show ip mroute vrf CISCO-CORP 232.1.1.1      ! NX-OS: same story
show ip pim group-range vrf CISCO-CORP       ! NX-OS: shows 232.0.0.0/8 = SSM
show ip igmp groups detail                   ! receiver: v3, include-mode, source 10.1.0.1
No (*,G), no Register, RP never consulted — that's the whole point of SSM, visible in one mroute.

docs.title: Part E — deliberate breaks
docs.text: Restore each break before moving to the next.

docs.title: E1 — RPF failover (the one that matters)
docs.text:
With the source pinging continuously (count 1000): 

! PBR-B — confirm current RPF path
show ip rpf 10.1.0.1                  ! expect via Gi3 / 10.20.60.1 (CSW2)

! Break it
interface GigabitEthernet3
 shutdown
Expected: a handful of lost replies, then the stream recovers. show ip rpf 10.1.0.1 now shows Gi2 / 10.20.30.1 — the (S,G) rebuilt through CSW1, driven purely by the unicast table changing. Confirm CSW1 now carries the (S,G) it didn't have before. no shutdown and note the tree doesn't necessarily swing back until state times out — RPF follows unicast, but PIM isn't in a hurry.

docs.title: E2 — SSM without IGMPv3
docs.text:
! NEXUS-B
interface Vlan10
  ip igmp version 2
Try the 232.1.1.1 stream again. Expected: dead. A v2 join can't express a source, and the SSM range refuses (*,G) state — check show ip mroute vrf CISCO-CORP 232.1.1.1 (nothing, or no OIF). This is the "SSM requires IGMPv3" exam fact, experienced. Restore ip igmp version 3.

docs.title: E3 — RP dependency (ASM vs SSM)
docs.text:
! PBR-B
no ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1
Expected: new joins to 239.1.1.10 fail (PBR-B can't map group→RP, no shared tree), while 232.1.1.1 keeps flowing — SSM has no RP to lose. Restore the rp-address before Part F.

docs.title: E4 — static mroute: steering RPF without touching unicast
docs.text:
The GRE tunnel is PIM-capable but OSPF-expensive, so it never wins RPF. Force it: 

! PBR-B — enable PIM on the tunnel (both ends)
interface Tunnel0
 ip pim sparse-mode
! (mirror on PBR-A Tunnel0)

! PBR-B — RPF for the source subnet now points into the tunnel
ip mroute 10.1.0.0 255.255.255.0 Tunnel0
Expected: show ip pim neighbor lists a neighbor on Tunnel0 (proof GRE carries multicast — native IPsec can't, GRE-over-IPsec can, a favourite exam distinction). show ip rpf 10.1.0.1 now says Tunnel0 via static mroute, and the (S,G) rebuilds through the tunnel while unicast still uses the physical path — RPF and unicast decoupled. Remove with no ip mroute 10.1.0.0 255.255.255.0 Tunnel0. Leave PIM on the tunnels; it's harmless and useful later. (Don't lower the tunnel's OSPF cost to achieve this instead — the tunnel destination is learned via the same OSPF, and you'll build a recursive-routing flap.)

docs.title: Part F — MSDP anycast-RP (the stretch that teaches why MSDP exists)
docs.text: Do this in the order written — the mid-point failure is the lesson.

docs.title: F1 — create the anycast condition (and watch ASM break)
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-B
interface Loopback100
 description RP-ANYCAST
 ip address 10.255.100.1 255.255.255.255
 ip pim sparse-mode
!
router ospf 1
 network 10.255.100.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
Two routers now advertise 10.255.100.1/32; everyone uses their closest RP. Source (NEXUS-A) registers to PBR-A; receiver (NEXUS-B) joins toward PBR-B. Start the 239.1.1.10 stream: it fails or goes one-way — PBR-B is an RP that has never heard of the source. show ip mroute 239.1.1.10 on PBR-B: (*,G) with receivers, no (S,G). That gap is precisely what MSDP fills.

docs.title: F2 — peer the RPs
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-A
interface Loopback101
 ip address 10.255.101.1 255.255.255.255
router ospf 1
 network 10.255.101.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
ip msdp peer 10.255.101.2 connect-source Loopback101
ip msdp originator-id Loopback101

! CORP-PBR-B
interface Loopback101
 ip address 10.255.101.2 255.255.255.255
router ospf 1
 network 10.255.101.2 0.0.0.0 area 0
ip msdp peer 10.255.101.1 connect-source Loopback101
ip msdp originator-id Loopback101

show ip msdp summary        ! peer state Up (it's a TCP session, port 639)
show ip msdp sa-cache       ! on PBR-B once the source pings: (10.1.0.1, 239.1.1.10) learned from PBR-A
Expected: the moment the SA appears in PBR-B's cache, the stream completes. Register goes to one RP, MSDP tells the other, receiver-side RP joins toward the source.

docs.title: F3 — prove the redundancy
docs.text:
! CORP-PBR-A
interface Loopback100
 shutdown
Unicast reconverges, 10.255.100.1 now resolves to PBR-B everywhere, registration and joins shift there, stream survives. That's RP failover without touching a single client config. no shutdown after.

One-liner for the exam: NX-OS also offers a protocol-native alternative (ip pim anycast-rp, RFC 4610) that does this without MSDP — know it exists; MSDP is the one the blueprint names.

docs.title: Part G — BiDir PIM (describe-level, 10 minutes)
docs.text:
Consistent mapping everywhere, scoped to its own range:

! Both PBRs (IOS-XE)
ip pim bidir-enable
ip access-list standard BIDIR-GROUPS
 permit 239.200.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1 BIDIR-GROUPS bidir

! All four NX-OS boxes, under vrf context CISCO-CORP
  ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1 group-list 239.200.1.0/24 bidir

Join 239.200.1.1 on NEXUS-B Vlan10, ping it from NEXUS-A, then look: 

show ip pim rp mapping                        ! 239.200.1.0/24 -> Bidir Mode
show ip mroute 239.200.1.1                    ! (*,G) ONLY, B flag - even while traffic flows
The takeaway: traffic forwarding with no (S,G) state ever created — that's BiDir's entire value proposition (many-to-many with tiny state), and seeing the mroute makes it stick. Don't sink more time here; describe-level is all ENCOR asks.

docs.title: Troubleshooting quick hits
docs.text:
• Counters increment but no ping replies → normal on NX-OS join-group; trust show ip mroute ... detail / show ip mroute count. Put the join back on PBR-B Gi1 if you want replies.
  • No (S,G) anywhere → check the FHR: does NEXUS-A's Vlan10 have ip pim sparse-mode? No PIM on the source interface = no Register.
  • (*,G) exists, (S,G) RPF-fails → show ip rpf <source> hop by hop; nine times out of ten it's the ECMP pin on the "wrong" core switch or a missing sparse-mode on that path.
  • PIM neighbor missing on one link → show ip pim interface both ends; on NX-OS confirm feature pim actually enabled.

docs.title: Rollback (complete removal)
docs.text:
! PBR-A / PBR-B
no ip msdp peer <peer>            (F)
no interface Loopback100          (A/F)
no interface Loopback101          (F)
no ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1
no ip pim rp-address 10.255.100.1 BIDIR-GROUPS bidir
no ip pim ssm default
no ip pim bidir-enable
no ip mroute 10.1.0.0 255.255.255.0 Tunnel0
no ip multicast-routing distributed
! plus: no ip pim sparse-mode / no ip igmp ... under Gi1-3, Tunnel0
! and remove the two Loopback network statements under router ospf 1

! All four NX-OS boxes
no feature pim                    ! removes every pim/igmp interface + vrf command in one go

docs.title: Checklist mapping
docs.text: ENCOR line Where you did it PIM-SM Parts A–B (Register/Register-Stop watched live) IGMPv2 Parts B–C IGMPv3 Part D receiver config SSM Part D + break E2 Bidirectional PIM Part G MSDP Part F (anycast-RP, break-then-fix) Conditional debug (bonus) Part B step 2 RPF / static mroute (bonus) E1, E4

docs.title: Phase 3 — Assurance & Automation: QoS, NetFlow, RESTCONF, AAA, CoPP
docs.text:
Five checklist lines, mostly on the PBR-A / LibreNMS pair plus Q-EDGE and one canary switch. Grounded in your current export: PBR-A already runs ip http secure-server + ip http authentication local, Gi4 is unused (our safe API-write target), Q-SW39 has no aaa new-model yet, and LibreNMS's existing SNMP polling will exercise the CoPP counters for free.

Time budget: A+B one evening (they share test traffic), C one evening, D+E one evening.

One hygiene observation before starting: the fleet runs username admin privilege 15 password 0 REMOVED — plaintext type-0. Parts C and D introduce properly-secured accounts; a fleet-wide secret conversion is worth a later pass, but don't change the admin password mid-phase (Oxidized and your own SSH ride on it).

docs.title: Part A — QoS: the full classify → mark → queue → shape chain
docs.text:
The guide's policy, but with the piece most labs skip: an ingress marking policy, so the egress queuing has something real to act on, and a parent shaper to manufacture congestion — without congestion, LLQ and bandwidth guarantees are dormant and the counters prove nothing.

Traffic simulation: ICMP plays "voice" (marked EF), SSH plays "business" (marked AF31).

docs.title: A.1 Ingress marking — CORP-PBR-A
docs.text:
ip access-list extended QOS-VOICE-SIM
 permit icmp any any
ip access-list extended QOS-BUSINESS-SIM
 permit tcp any any eq 22
 permit tcp any eq 22 any
!
class-map match-any MARK-VOICE
 match access-group name QOS-VOICE-SIM
class-map match-any MARK-BUSINESS
 match access-group name QOS-BUSINESS-SIM
!
policy-map MARK-IN
 class MARK-VOICE
  set dscp ef
 class MARK-BUSINESS
  set dscp af31
!
interface GigabitEthernet1
 service-policy input MARK-IN

docs.title: A.2 Egress queuing under a shaper — CORP-PBR-A
docs.text:
Both Gi2 and Gi3 get it, because your PBR splits VLAN20 traffic to CSW1 and VLAN40 to CSW2:

class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
class-map match-any BUSINESS
 match dscp af31
!
policy-map WAN-OUT
 class VOICE
  priority percent 20
 class BUSINESS
  bandwidth percent 30
 class class-default
  fair-queue
!
policy-map WAN-SHAPE
 class class-default
  shape average 1000000
  service-policy WAN-OUT
!
interface GigabitEthernet2
 service-policy output WAN-SHAPE
interface GigabitEthernet3
 service-policy output WAN-SHAPE

The parent shapes everything to 1 Mbps; the child divides that 1 Mbps. So priority percent 20 = a 200 kbps LLQ policer — small enough to hit with pings.

Heads-up: while WAN-SHAPE is applied, all inter-site CORP traffic (tunnels included) is capped at 1 Mbps. Management via the DMZ path (Gi1.99) is unaffected. Remove the shaper when done.

docs.title: A.3 Drive traffic and read the counters
docs.text:
! NEXUS-A — "voice" flood (EF):
ping 10.2.1.1 vrf CISCO-CORP source 10.2.0.1 count 500 packet-size 1400

! NEXUS-A — "business" (AF31): the TCP handshake is the traffic; login not required
ssh admin@10.1.1.1 vrf CISCO-CORP

! CORP-PBR-A
show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet1 input     ! MARK-VOICE / MARK-BUSINESS packet counts
show policy-map interface GigabitEthernet2 output    ! parent shaper stats + child classes

What to look for on the egress side: the parent class shows target/average rate 1000000 and — during the flood — a non-zero queue depth. Under the child, VOICE shows offered packets and drops: 1400-byte pings at speed exceed 200 kbps, and the LLQ policer discards the excess. That's the guide's line "strict priority capped to prevent starvation" as a live counter — priority traffic gets absolute preference up to its cap, then drops rather than starving BUSINESS and class-default.

docs.title: A.4 Break — remove the trust
docs.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1
 no service-policy input MARK-IN

Re-run the flood: VOICE class counters on Gi2 freeze; everything lands in class-default. Downstream queuing is only as good as upstream marking — that's the trust-boundary concept in one move. Re-apply MARK-IN.

docs.title: A.5 Steady state
docs.text: Remove the shaper after the exercise (no service-policy output WAN-SHAPE on Gi2/Gi3). Keep or remove the class-maps/policies as you like — reading them back is Week-3 revision material. Leave MARK-IN applied if you're doing Part B next; NetFlow will report the DSCP values it sets.

docs.title: Part B — Flexible NetFlow → your existing Akvorado
docs.text: You already run a collector: Akvorado's inlet listens on UDP 2055 by default (confirm the port mapping in its docker-compose on the LibreNMS box). Export goes out the DMZ management path — same route SNMP already proves works.

docs.title: B.1 Configure — CORP-PBR-A
docs.text:
flow record FNF-RECORD
 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address
 match transport source-port
 match transport destination-port
 match ip protocol
 match interface input
 collect ipv4 dscp
 collect counter bytes long
 collect counter packets long
 collect timestamp sys-uptime first
 collect timestamp sys-uptime last
!
flow exporter FNF-EXPORTER
 destination 10.99.0.12 vrf DMZ
 source Loopback99
 transport udp 2055
 export-protocol netflow-v9
!
flow monitor FNF-MONITOR
 record FNF-RECORD
 exporter FNF-EXPORTER
 cache timeout active 60
 cache timeout inactive 15
!
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input

(collect ipv4 dscp is the Part A tie-in — flows arrive pre-marking on Gi1 input, so you'll see the original DSCP; move the monitor to Gi2 output later if you want to see EF/AF31 post-marking. If your release rejects the vrf DMZ keyword on the destination, drop the exporter lines and run cache-only — the checklist line is still fully covered.)

docs.title: B.2 Generate and verify
docs.text:
Re-run the Part A traffic, then:

show flow monitor FNF-MONITOR cache format table   ! flows: src/dst, ports, proto, counters
show flow exporter FNF-EXPORTER statistics         ! export packets sent, no errors
show running-config | section flow                 ! the guide's own verification

Expected in the cache: your ICMP flood as proto 1 flows, the SSH attempt as proto 6 dst-port 22, byte/packet counters climbing. On the collector side, check Akvorado's UI for a new exporter at 10.99.250.250; fallback if Akvorado isn't listening:

# LibreNMS box
sudo apt install nfdump
sudo nfcapd -D -p 2055 -l /tmp/nfcap        # only if 2055 is free
nfdump -R /tmp/nfcap -o extended | head

Flow accounting vs packet capture, the exam distinction: the cache shows who talked to whom, how much — never payload.

docs.title: Part C — RESTCONF and NETCONF on IOS-XE
docs.text: PBR-A is one command from RESTCONF-ready. Create a dedicated API account rather than reusing admin:

docs.title: C.1 Enable — CORP-PBR-A
docs.text:
username api privilege 15 secret REMOVED
restconf
netconf-yang

Optional hygiene while here: no ip http server (plain HTTP is on fleet-wide; RESTCONF only needs the secure server).

show netconf-yang status                  ! netconf-yang: enabled, ssh port 830
show ip http server secure status

docs.title: C.2 Read via RESTCONF — from the LibreNMS box
docs.text:
Target the DMZ management loopback (10.99.250.250) — the path your NMS already uses:

curl -k -u api:REMOVED -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  https://10.99.250.250/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces

curl -k -u api:REMOVED -H "Accept: application/yang-data+json" \
  https://10.99.250.250/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet1

Expected: JSON — name, description, type, enabled — for every interface. Put it next to show ip interface brief on the router (the guide's task): same truth, machine-readable.

docs.title: C.3 Write via RESTCONF — the part that makes it click
docs.text:
Gi4 is unused, so it's a safe target:

curl -k -u api:REMOVED -X PATCH -H "Content-Type: application/yang-data+json" \
  https://10.99.250.250/restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet4 \
  -d '{"ietf-interfaces:interface":{"name":"GigabitEthernet4","description":"SET-BY-RESTCONF"}}'

Expect 204 No Content (silent success), then on the router: show running-config interface GigabitEthernet4 — the description is there. You've configured IOS-XE without touching the CLI. Clean up by PATCHing a new description or no description conventionally.

docs.title: C.4 NETCONF — see the other protocol's shape
docs.text:
# LibreNMS box
ssh -p 830 api@10.99.250.250 -s netconf

Expected: a wall of XML — the <hello> with capability list. That contrast is the exam table: RESTCONF = HTTPS/JSON/REST-style, NETCONF = SSH-830/XML/RPC, same YANG models underneath. Ctrl-C out. If the port times out on the DMZ path while RESTCONF works, you've met a real IOS-XE quirk — NETCONF listening only in the global VRF on some releases. Note it and move on; RESTCONF covers the configure-and-verify line.

docs.title: C.5 Breaks (two minutes)
docs.text: Wrong password → HTTP 401. no restconf → connection refused, restconf to restore. The REST-API-security checklist line maps here: HTTPS transport, least-privilege accounts, no -k in production (validate certs), no hard-coded secrets.

docs.title: Part D — AAA: TACACS+ device administration
docs.text:
Server is tac_plus on the LibreNMS Ubuntu (10.99.0.12). Canary device is Q-SW39 — its mgmt SVI reaches 10.99.0.12 over the same DMZ path SNMP already uses. If your ISE VM boots, everything below is identical except the server address and key.

Safety rule for this part: keep a working SSH session AND the console open on Q-SW39 until the break test passes. Console authentication is untouched throughout.

docs.title: D.1 Server — LibreNMS box
docs.text:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install tacacs+
sudo nano /etc/tacacs+/tac_plus.conf

Minimal config (replace the file's example content):

key = REMOVED

user = quser {
    login = cleartext REMOVED
    service = exec {
        priv-lvl = 15
    }
}

sudo systemctl restart tacacs_plus
sudo systemctl status tacacs_plus
ss -ltn | grep :49          ! listening on tcp/49

docs.title: D.2 Canary — Q-SW39
docs.text:
Order matters: pin the local safety net before anything else.

aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default local
!
tacacs server LNMS-TAC
 address ipv4 10.99.0.12
 key REMOVED
!
aaa group server tacacs+ TAC-GROUP
 server name LNMS-TAC
!
aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group TAC-GROUP local
aaa authorization exec VTY-AUTHZ group TAC-GROUP local
aaa accounting exec VTY-ACCT start-stop group TAC-GROUP
!
ip tacacs source-interface Vlan99
!
line vty 0 4
 login authentication VTY-AUTH
 authorization exec VTY-AUTHZ
 accounting exec VTY-ACCT

(Named method lists on the vty only — console and default stay local. That's the lockout-proof pattern. Adjust the source-interface if your mgmt SVI is named differently.)

docs.title: D.3 Verify
docs.text:
test aaa group TAC-GROUP quser REMOVED legacy    ! "User successfully authenticated"
show tacacs                                          ! socket opens, request/response counters

Fresh SSH to Q-SW39 as quser → straight to # (priv 15 from the server's exec authorization — no enable password needed: that's authorization doing its job, distinct from authentication). On the server, watch accounting arrive:

sudo tail -f /var/log/tac_plus.acct     # or: sudo journalctl -u tacacs_plus -f

Start/stop records with username, line, and source — the third A, live.

docs.title: D.4 The break that earns your trust — fallback proof
docs.text:
Before rolling TACACS to more devices, prove the local at the end of the method lists actually catches you:

# LibreNMS box
sudo systemctl stop tacacs_plus

New SSH to Q-SW39: quser now fails (server dead, no local quser), but admin succeeds after a short server-timeout pause — the method list walked group TAC-GROUP → dead → local → matched. That pause-then-local-login signature is what a TACACS outage looks like in production. sudo systemctl start tacacs_plus, confirm quser works again.

Once trusted, replicating to the fleet is a paste of D.2 per device.

docs.title: Part E — CoPP: build one, inspect one
E.1 Build — Q-EDGE (IOS)
docs.text:
Q-EDGE's control plane now sees OSPF (two VRFs), PIM and IGMP (your Site Q multicast extension), SSH, SNMP from LibreNMS, and ICMP. Three classes: routing protected absolutely, management policed, everything else measured:

ip access-list extended COPP-MGMT
 permit tcp 10.99.0.0 0.0.255.255 any eq 22
 permit udp 10.99.0.0 0.0.255.255 any eq 161
 permit icmp 10.99.0.0 0.0.255.255 any
ip access-list extended COPP-ROUTING
 permit ospf any any
 permit pim any any
 permit igmp any any
!
class-map match-any COPP-ROUTING-CLASS
 match access-group name COPP-ROUTING
class-map match-any COPP-MGMT-CLASS
 match access-group name COPP-MGMT
!
policy-map COPP-POLICY
 class COPP-ROUTING-CLASS
 class COPP-MGMT-CLASS
  police 64000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
 class class-default
  police 256000 conform-action transmit exceed-action transmit
!
control-plane
 service-policy input COPP-POLICY

Design notes worth internalising: the ROUTING class carries no police statement — classify-and-transmit, because a mis-sized policer here drops hellos and takes down adjacencies (the guide's production warning, engineered out). class-default polices with transmit/transmit — monitor mode: counts what would exceed, drops nothing, exactly how you'd stage CoPP in production before enforcing.

docs.title: E.2 Verify
docs.text:
show policy-map control-plane

Expected within a minute, no effort: COPP-MGMT-CLASS conform counters climbing (LibreNMS SNMP polls), COPP-ROUTING-CLASS counting OSPF/PIM hellos steadily. SSH in from the NMS box and watch your own session tick the counter.

docs.title: E.3 Break — feel the policer
docs.text:
policy-map COPP-POLICY
 class COPP-MGMT-CLASS
  police 8000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop

From the LibreNMS box: ping 10.99.2.1 -i 0.01 -s 1000 (fast, big). Expected: heavy loss on the ping, exceeded ... drop counters climbing in show policy-map control-plane — and note your SSH session getting sluggish, because it shares the class. CoPP protects the CPU from management traffic including yours — the double edge the guide warns about. Restore police 64000.

Recovery note: if you ever wedge management entirely, the EVE-NG console is unaffected — control-plane → no service-policy input COPP-POLICY.

docs.title: E.4 Inspect — the N9Kv contrast
docs.text:
NX-OS refuses to run without CoPP; it shipped attached before you configured anything:

! CSW1
show copp status                                        ! copp-system-p-policy-strict attached
show policy-map interface control-plane | i class-map|violate

Scroll the class list — management, IGMP, routing protocols, ARP, all pre-classified with per-class policers, and violated counters showing anything already being dropped. IOS makes you build CoPP; NX-OS makes you tune it — a tidy exam contrast, and the reason a default N9K survives abuse a default ISR wouldn't.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: A: no service-policy (input Gi1, output Gi2/Gi3), then no policy-map MARK-IN / WAN-OUT / WAN-SHAPE, no class-map ..., no ip access-list extended QOS-*. B: no ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input on Gi1, then no flow monitor / exporter / record. C: no restconf, no netconf-yang, no username api. D: on Q-SW39 remove the three list applications under vty, then the lists, group, server, and (last) no aaa new-model; sudo apt remove tacacs+ on the box. E: control-plane → no service-policy input COPP-POLICY, then remove policy/classes/ACLs. (Don't touch the N9Kv's system policy.)

docs.title: Checklist mapping
docs.text: ENCOR line Where QoS config interpretation Part A (marking, LLQ cap drops, shaping vs policing, trust boundary) Flexible NetFlow Part B (record/exporter/monitor, cache + collector, DSCP visibility) NETCONF and RESTCONF Part C (read, write via PATCH, both protocol shapes) REST API security C.5 (transport, least privilege, cert validation, secrets) AAA authentication & authorisation Part D (named lists, priv-15 authz, accounting, fallback proven) ACLs / CoPP Part E (build + break on IOS, inspect defaults on NX-OS)

docs.title: Side Phase — TACACS+, RADIUS and Authenticator-App OTP
docs.text:
Three engines, each doing the job it's actually good at:

Engine Where Job tac_plus (built from source) Ubuntu 10.99.0.12 Simple TACACS+ — the protocol, bare. Your fallback and reference. FreeRADIUS + Google Authenticator PAM Ubuntu 10.99.0.12 The OTP engine. This is what your phone talks to. Cisco ISE Gret A, mgmt segment The policy engine — per-command authorization, and a front-end that can proxy to the OTP engine.

The headline flow you're building:

You ──SSH──► Q-SW39 ──TACACS+──► ISE ──proxy──► FreeRADIUS ──PAM──► Google Authenticator (TOTP)
                                   │
                                   └──► shell profile (priv 15) + command set (what you may type)

Login with a 6-digit code from your phone and get per-command authorization. That's genuinely enterprise-grade, and it's four parts away.

Time budget: Part 0 = 10 min. Part A+B = one evening (this is the OTP payoff). Part C = one evening. Part D = one evening. Parts E/F when curious.

docs.title: Two facts to internalise before touching anything
docs.text:
1. TOTP only works over PAP. The OTP is validated by PAM, which needs the plaintext token. VTY login over RADIUS sends PAP — fine. EAP-based 802.1X cannot do TOTP this way (EAP methods derive keys from a stored credential; there's nothing for PAM to check). So: OTP for device admin login, certificates/PEAP for network access. That's not a lab limitation, that's how the protocols work — and it's a great exam-level distinction.

2. Method lists fall through on NO RESPONSE, not on REJECT. aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group RAD-GROUP local tries RADIUS; if RADIUS says reject, that's authoritative and you're done — it does not try local. Only a dead/unreachable server advances to the next method. This is why you never mix two live auth servers in one list hoping for "try both".

Safety rule for the entire phase: keep a console session open on Q-SW39 at all times. By default IOS exempts the console from aaa authorization, so the console is your escape hatch even if you break command authorization completely. Never remove local from the end of a method list.

docs.title: Part 0 — finish tac_plus (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Your daemon builds and starts, then systemd kills it: tac_plus forks to background, systemd sees the parent exit, sends SIGTERM to the child. Keep it in the foreground.

sudo systemctl stop tac_plus
sudo sed -i 's|tac_plus -C|tac_plus -G -C|' /etc/systemd/system/tac_plus.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start tac_plus
sudo systemctl status tac_plus        # want: active (running), NOT "inactive (dead)"
ss -ltnp | grep :49

If tac_plus -G errors with an illegal option, your build doesn't have the foreground flag — use Type=forking instead: add Type=forking under [Service], leave ExecStart without -G, daemon-reload, restart.

Validate the config file any time with: tac_plus -P -C /etc/tacacs+/tac_plus.conf

Firewall — the box now needs three ports open. Check and allow: 

sudo ufw status
# if active:
sudo ufw allow 49/tcp comment 'TACACS+'
sudo ufw allow 1812/udp comment 'RADIUS auth'
sudo ufw allow 1813/udp comment 'RADIUS acct'

Then re-test from Q-SW39: 

ping 10.99.0.12 source vlan99
test aaa group TAC-GROUP quser REMOVED legacy      ! want: User successfully authenticated
show tacacs                                            ! socket opens / requests / responses

If the ping works but the test still fails, check show run | inc tacacs — key must be exactly REMOVED, and ip tacacs source-interface Vlan99 must be set so the switch sources from an address the server can reply to.

docs.title: Part A — FreeRADIUS + Google Authenticator (the OTP engine)
A.1 Time sync — do this first, not last
docs.text:
TOTP is a function of the clock. Skew is the number-one cause of "wrong code" failures, and it fails in a way that looks like a config error.

timedatectl                      # want: "System clock synchronized: yes"
sudo timedatectl set-ntp true

Your phone must also be on network time (Settings → Date & Time → Automatic). A window of ±90s is what we'll configure, which is forgiving but not infinite.

docs.title: A.2 Install
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install freeradius freeradius-utils libpam-google-authenticator

(FreeRADIUS on Ubuntu 24.04 is 3.2.x, but the config directory is still called 3.0 — that's normal, not a mistake.)

docs.title: A.3 Create the OTP user and enrol your phone
docs.text:
The FreeRADIUS daemon runs as user freerad, so the secret must live somewhere freerad can read. Central directory, not a home dir:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth
sudo chmod 700 /etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth

sudo google-authenticator -t -d -f -r 3 -R 30 -w 3 -e 5 \
     -s /etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth/netadmin

Flags: -t time-based, -d disallow code reuse, -f write without prompting, -r 3 -R 30 rate-limit 3 attempts per 30s, -w 3 allow ±1 window (~90s skew), -e 5 emergency scratch codes.

A QR code prints in the terminal. Scan it with Google Authenticator / Authy / Microsoft Authenticator / 1Password — any TOTP app. Copy the emergency scratch codes somewhere safe — they're single-use logins if you lose the phone.

Now hand the file to the daemon:

sudo chown -R freerad:freerad /etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth
sudo chmod 600 /etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth/netadmin

docs.title: A.4 Wire PAM
docs.text:
Replace /etc/pam.d/radiusd entirely — OTP-only to start (you type just the 6 digits as your password). We add the static password in A.7 once the mechanism is proven.

sudo tee /etc/pam.d/radiusd << 'EOF'
auth       required     pam_google_authenticator.so secret=/etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth/${USER} allowed_perm=0600
account    required     pam_permit.so
session    required     pam_permit.so
EOF

${USER} is expanded by the PAM module, so one line serves every user you enrol later.

docs.title: A.5 Enable the PAM module in FreeRADIUS
docs.text:
sudo ln -s /etc/freeradius/3.0/mods-available/pam /etc/freeradius/3.0/mods-enabled/pam

Then uncomment pam in the authenticate {} section of /etc/freeradius/3.0/sites-available/default:

sudo nano /etc/freeradius/3.0/sites-available/default
Find the authenticate { block and remove the # from the line that is just pam.

docs.title: A.6 User and client
docs.text:
Add the user at the top of /etc/freeradius/3.0/mods-config/files/authorize (above the DEFAULT entries — first match wins):

netadmin  Auth-Type := PAM
          Service-Type = NAS-Prompt-User,
          Cisco-AVPair = "shell:priv-lvl=15"

Auth-Type := PAM sends this user down the PAM stack you just built. The reply attributes are what drop you straight to # — RADIUS's equivalent of a TACACS+ shell profile.

Add your lab as a client in /etc/freeradius/3.0/clients.conf:

client lab-mgmt {
        ipaddr = 10.99.0.0/16
        secret = REMOVED
        nas_type = cisco
        shortname = lab
}

(One subnet entry covers every device that sources from the mgmt/DMZ range — adjust the prefix if your devices source elsewhere. Leave the shipped client localhost alone; the next step uses it.)

docs.title: A.7 Test locally — before any switch is involved
docs.text:
Run FreeRADIUS in the foreground so you can watch the auth happen. This is the single most useful FreeRADIUS skill there is:

sudo systemctl stop freeradius
sudo freeradius -X

In a second SSH session, with a fresh code from your phone:

radtest netadmin 123456 127.0.0.1 0 testing123

Expected: Received Access-Accept, carrying Service-Type and Cisco-AVPair. In the -X window you'll see the PAM module called and pam_authenticate: Success. Try again with the same code — it should now fail (that's -d, replay protection, working).

Common -X failures and what they mean: - PAM: Cannot open ... Permission denied → the chown/chmod in A.3 didn't take - Invalid verification code → clock skew (recheck timedatectl), or you fat-fingered it - Auth-Type PAM not found → the symlink in A.5 or the pam line in sites-available/default

Once it works: Ctrl-C, then sudo systemctl start freeradius.

docs.title: Part B — Canary: OTP login on Q-SW39
B.1 Switch config
docs.text:
radius server LNMS-RAD
 address ipv4 10.99.0.12 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
 key REMOVED
!
aaa group server radius RAD-GROUP
 server name LNMS-RAD
!
ip radius source-interface Vlan99
!
aaa authentication login VTY-OTP group RAD-GROUP local
aaa authorization exec VTY-OTP-AUTHZ group RAD-GROUP local
!
line vty 0 4
 login authentication VTY-OTP
 authorization exec VTY-OTP-AUTHZ

Note the explicit ports. Cisco's historic default is 1645/1646; FreeRADIUS listens on 1812/1813. Omit auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813 and you get silent timeouts — a classic.

Test without risking your session: 

test aaa group RAD-GROUP netadmin <6-digit-code> new-code

docs.title: B.2 The login
docs.text:
SSH to Q-SW39 as netadmin. At the password prompt, type the 6-digit code from your phone. You should land straight at # (priv 15, courtesy of the Cisco-AVPair).

Stop and appreciate what just happened: the switch never knew about TOTP. It sent PAP to RADIUS; RADIUS asked PAM; PAM checked the shared secret against the clock. Zero changes to the AAA protocol — this is why token-based auth bolted onto RADIUS so easily in the 90s and still does.

docs.title: B.3 Upgrade to real two-factor (password + OTP)
docs.text:
Right now the phone is the only factor. True MFA = something you know + something you have. The RADIUS User-Password field carries one string, so the convention is password immediately followed by the code, with PAM splitting them:

# Give netadmin a system password to check against:
sudo useradd -M -s /usr/sbin/nologin netadmin 2>/dev/null
sudo passwd netadmin

# freerad must be able to read /etc/shadow to verify it:
sudo usermod -a -G shadow freerad

sudo tee /etc/pam.d/radiusd << 'EOF'
auth       requisite    pam_google_authenticator.so forward_pass secret=/etc/freeradius/3.0/googleauth/${USER} allowed_perm=0600
auth       required     pam_unix.so use_first_pass
account    required     pam_permit.so
session    required     pam_permit.so
EOF

sudo systemctl restart freeradius

forward_pass tells the OTP module to strip the trailing 6 digits, validate them, and hand the remainder to pam_unix as the password. So at the switch's password prompt you now type REMOVED — password then code, no space.

Test: radtest netadmin 'REMOVED' 127.0.0.1 0 testing123

Security note, stated honestly: adding freerad to the shadow group lets the RADIUS daemon read every password hash on the box. Acceptable in a lab; in production you'd point PAM at a dedicated credential store (LDAP/SSSD) instead. Know the tradeoff you're making — that's the REST-API-security mindset applied to AAA.

docs.title: B.4 Breaks
docs.text: Break Do it Expected Replay Log in with a code, immediately log in again with the same code Rejected — -d blocks reuse. This is why TOTP resists shoulder-surfing. Clock skew sudo timedatectl set-ntp false && sudo date -s "+5 minutes" Every code fails. Restore with set-ntp true. Now you'll recognise this failure instead of debugging config for an hour. Server down sudo systemctl stop freeradius netadmin fails; admin still works via local after a timeout pause. The fallback is real. Restart after. Reject ≠ fallthrough With FreeRADIUS running, SSH as a username it doesn't know Rejected outright — IOS does not try local. This is the fact from the top of the doc, felt.

docs.title: Part C — ISE: the policy engine (per-command authorization)
docs.text:
tac_plus authenticates. ISE decides what you're allowed to type. That's the TACACS+ superpower RADIUS doesn't have — and it's the exam point.

ISE GUI paths drift between 3.x releases; treat these as approximate and navigate by name. The verification at C.5 is the ground truth.

docs.title: C.1 Enable Device Admin
docs.text:
• Administration → System → Licensing — confirm a Device Admin license is present (the eval covers it).
  • Administration → System → Deployment → your node → Edit → tick Enable Device Admin Service → Save. (ISE will restart services — this takes a while. Go make tea.)

docs.title: C.2 Add Q-SW39 as a network device
docs.text: Administration → Network Resources → Network Devices → Add - Name Q-SW39, IP = Q-SW39's Vlan99 address - Tick TACACS+ Authentication Settings → Shared Secret: REMOVED

docs.title: C.3 Two users, two roles
docs.text: Administration → Identity Management → Identities → Users → Add — create: - netops-admin (put it in a group, e.g. Network Admins) - netops-ro (group e.g. Network Read Only)

docs.title: C.4 The results objects
docs.text:
Work Centers → Device Administration → Policy Elements → Results:

  • TACACS Profiles → Add: Shell-Priv15 — Common Task Type = Shell, Default Privilege 15, Maximum Privilege 15.
  • TACACS Profiles → Add: Shell-Priv1 — Default Privilege 1, Maximum 1.
  • TACACS Command Sets → Add: CMD-ReadOnly — leave "Permit any command that is not listed below" unticked, then permit only:
  • show (arguments: .*)
  • ping (arguments: .*)
  • exit
  • TACACS Command Sets → Add: CMD-Full — tick "Permit any command that is not listed below".

docs.title: C.5 The policy set
docs.text: Work Centers → Device Administration → Device Admin Policy Sets → Add - Name Lab-DeviceAdmin, condition: Device Type / Network Device Name matches your lab (or just Any for now) - Authentication Policy: Identity Source = Internal Users - Authorization Policy — two rules: - netops-admin in Network Admins → Shell Profile Shell-Priv15 + Command Set CMD-Full - netops-ro in Network Read Only → Shell Profile Shell-Priv1 + Command Set CMD-ReadOnly

docs.title: C.6 Point Q-SW39 at ISE — with command authorization
docs.text:
tacacs server ISE-TAC
 address ipv4 <ISE-IP>
 key REMOVED
!
aaa group server tacacs+ ISE-GROUP
 server name ISE-TAC
!
aaa authentication login VTY-ISE group ISE-GROUP local
aaa authorization exec VTY-ISE-AUTHZ group ISE-GROUP local
aaa authorization commands 15 CMD-AUTHZ group ISE-GROUP local
aaa authorization commands 1 CMD-AUTHZ1 group ISE-GROUP local
aaa accounting commands 15 CMD-ACCT start-stop group ISE-GROUP
!
line vty 0 4
 login authentication VTY-ISE
 authorization exec VTY-ISE-AUTHZ
 authorization commands 15 CMD-AUTHZ
 authorization commands 1 CMD-AUTHZ1
 accounting commands 15 CMD-ACCT

This is the one that can bite. Command authorization means every command you type is a TACACS+ round trip. If ISE misbehaves, your VTY session becomes read-only or worse. Console is exempt (no aaa authorization console configured) — that's your way back in. local on the end means an ISE outage degrades to local authorization rather than a lockout.

docs.title: C.7 The demo — this is the moment
docs.text:
Two SSH sessions:

! as netops-admin
Q-SW39# conf t                         ← works

! as netops-ro
Q-SW39> show ip interface brief        ← works
Q-SW39> ping 10.99.0.12                ← works
Q-SW39> conf t
Command authorization failed.          ← ✅ THE POINT

Then look at Operations → TACACS → Live Logs in ISE: every command, per user, per device, accepted or denied. That is exactly why TACACS+ owns device administration and RADIUS doesn't — RADIUS authorizes the session, TACACS+ authorizes every command, and it accounts for them individually.

docs.title: Part D — the crown: OTP through ISE, with command authorization
docs.text: Now join the two halves. ISE can use an external RADIUS Token Server as its identity source — that's how enterprises wire RSA SecurID in, and FreeRADIUS-with-TOTP slots into exactly the same socket.

docs.title: D.1 FreeRADIUS: trust ISE as a client
docs.text:
Add to /etc/freeradius/3.0/clients.conf (if ISE isn't already inside the 10.99.0.0/16 block from A.6, add it explicitly):

client ise {
        ipaddr = <ISE-IP>
        secret = REMOVED
        shortname = ise
}

sudo systemctl restart freeradius

docs.title: D.2 ISE: define the token server
docs.text: Administration → Identity Management → External Identity Sources → RADIUS Token → Add - Name: FREERAD-OTP - Connection tab: Host IP 10.99.0.12, Shared Secret REMOVED, Authentication Port 1812 - Save, then use the Test Connection button if your version offers one.

docs.title: D.3 Sequence it, then use it
docs.text:
Administration → Identity Management → Identity Source Sequences → Add - Name SEQ-OTP, add FREERAD-OTP to the authentication search list.

Then in your Lab-DeviceAdmin policy set: - Authentication Policy → change Identity Source from Internal Users to SEQ-OTP - Allowed Protocols must permit PAP/ASCII (TACACS+ ASCII login carries the password in the clear to ISE, which is exactly what lets ISE forward it to the token server) - Authorization Policy → the netadmin user needs a rule → give it Shell-Priv15 + CMD-Full (or CMD-ReadOnly if you want an OTP-protected read-only role — arguably the most realistic combination of all)

docs.title: D.4 Verify
docs.text:
SSH to Q-SW39 as netadmin, password = REMOVED (password + code, per B.3).

What happens: switch → TACACS+ → ISE → RADIUS/PAP → FreeRADIUS → PAM → TOTP validated → back up the chain → ISE applies shell profile and command set. You are logged in with a phone code and ISE is authorizing every command you type.

Watch it in Operations → TACACS → Live Logs — the authentication shows the external identity store in the detail view.

If your ISE version won't accept a RADIUS Token source for a device admin policy set (some releases restrict token servers to RADIUS/network-access policy sets), don't fight it: keep OTP on the direct Q-SW39→FreeRADIUS path from Part B, and keep ISE for command authorization. You've still built and understood both halves — and "the product wouldn't do X, so I designed around it" is a better interview story than a clean happy path.

docs.title: Part E — fleet rollout (the safe pattern)
docs.text:
Never roll AAA to the fleet in one go. Per device:

  1. Add the device in ISE (Network Devices) with the shared secret.
  2. Paste the C.6 block, adjusting <source-interface> to that device's mgmt SVI/loopback.
  3. Before logging out, from your existing session: test aaa group ISE-GROUP netops-admin <password> new-code
  4. Open a second SSH session and log in as netops-admin. Only when that works, close the first.
  5. local stays on every method list, forever. Non-negotiable.

NX-OS differs (feature tacacs+, tacacs-server host … key …, aaa authentication login default group ISE-GROUP local) — worth doing on one Nexus just to meet the syntax, since your estate is multi-OS and the exam is IOS-flavoured.

docs.title: Part F — stretch: 802.1X (RADIUS network access)
docs.text:
This is where RADIUS earns its keep, and where TOTP explicitly cannot follow (see the top of the doc).

On an access port: 

aaa authentication dot1x default group RAD-GROUP
aaa authorization network default group RAD-GROUP
dot1x system-auth-control
!
interface <access-port>
 authentication port-control auto
 authentication host-mode single-host
 mab
 dot1x pae authenticator
 spanning-tree portfast

Honest caveats: you need a real supplicant — VPCS can't do 802.1X. Use the Linux node with wpa_supplicant (EAP-MD5 is easiest against FreeRADIUS; PEAP needs a server cert). If that's too much yak-shaving, MAB (MAC Authentication Bypass) demonstrates the RADIUS network-access flow with no supplicant at all: FreeRADIUS just needs a users-file entry keyed on the MAC. For ENCOR, understanding the flow and the role of the authenticator/supplicant/auth-server triangle matters more than a working supplicant.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
! Q-SW39 — remove applications first, then the objects
line vty 0 4
 no authorization commands 15 CMD-AUTHZ
 no authorization commands 1 CMD-AUTHZ1
 no authorization exec VTY-ISE-AUTHZ
 no login authentication VTY-ISE
 login authentication default
!
no aaa authorization commands 15 CMD-AUTHZ
no aaa authorization commands 1 CMD-AUTHZ1
no aaa authentication login VTY-ISE
no aaa authentication login VTY-OTP
no aaa group server radius RAD-GROUP
no radius server LNMS-RAD
no tacacs server ISE-TAC

# Ubuntu
sudo systemctl disable --now freeradius tac_plus
sudo gpasswd -d freerad shadow          # undo the shadow-group grant
ISE: disable the policy set rather than deleting objects — you'll want them again.

docs.title: Checklist mapping
docs.text: ENCOR line Where AAA authentication Parts A, B (RADIUS+PAP+TOTP), C (TACACS+ via ISE) AAA authorisation C.4–C.7 — shell profiles, command sets, per-command authz AAA accounting C.6 (aaa accounting commands 15) + ISE Live Logs TACACS+ vs RADIUS The whole phase — you build both and feel why device admin uses one and network access the other ACLs / CoPP tie-in The COPP-MGMT class in Phase 3 already protects tcp/49 and udp/1812 — now it's protecting something real REST API security (MFA, least privilege) B.3 security note, C.4 read-only role TrustSec / ISE / endpoint Parts C–D give you first-hand ISE policy-engine experience — the describe-level topics stop being abstract 802.1X Part F

docs.title: What this adds to the story
docs.text: "I built TACACS+ from source, stood up FreeRADIUS with TOTP against Google Authenticator, and fronted both with ISE so that device logins take a phone code and every command is authorized per-role — then I proved the local fallback works by killing the servers." That's not a cert lab answer. That's an engineer's answer.

docs.title: Side Phase — Lab-Wide Flow Visibility
docs.text:
Goal: turn the single working exporter (CORP-PBR-A) into whole-estate visibility in Akvorado — both PBRs, Q-EDGE, and the two firewalls, with the NX-OS and IOS-XR boxes as honest stretch goals. By the end, the console's Exporter dimension becomes a map of your lab.

Time budget: Parts A+B one evening, Part C one evening, D is minutes, E when curious.

docs.title: Design principles (read once, they explain every choice below)
docs.text:
1. Input monitors on every routed interface of an instrumented device. That gives each device a complete view — every packet transiting it is seen exactly once on entry. No output monitors needed.

2. Cross-exporter duplication is inherent — don't fight it. A single A→B flow will be observed by PBR-A and PBR-B (and Q-EDGE if it transits Site Q). Akvorado does not deduplicate across exporters; that's by design — each exporter is an independent observation point. In the console, filter or group by Exporter when you want truth; understand that "all exporters" sums observations, not unique bytes.

3. Every new exporter must pass Akvorado's two gates (both verified in the 2.4.0 source): - SNMP metadata: the outlet polls the flow packets' source address with the credentials in outlet.yaml (REMOVED under ::/0). If the poll fails, flows are dropped with flows_errors_total{error="metadata missing"}. So every exporter must answer SNMP on the address it sources flows from — for the routers that's already true (LibreNMS polls them); for the firewalls it's a setup step. - Sampling rate: already insured — default-sampling-rate: 1 under ::/0 covers every unsampled exporter you add. sFlow and IOS-XR advertise their own rates, which override nothing (they simply arrive non-zero).

4. The flow record must carry interface indexes. Flows without ifIndex are dropped (input and output interfaces missing). Your FNF-RECORD has match interface input — keep it in every copy.

docs.title: A.1 CORP-PBR-A — extend to all routed interfaces
docs.text:
The record/exporter/monitor already exist; just widen the application:

interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input
interface GigabitEthernet3
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input
interface Tunnel0
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input

(Add Tunnel1 too once Phase 1 Task 3 is done.) Tunnel0 input is a fun one: it sees the decapsulated inner flows arriving over GRE — including your multicast — where Gi2 only ever sees ESP.

docs.title: A.2 CORP-PBR-B — full stack, mirrored
docs.text:
flow record FNF-RECORD
 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address
 match transport source-port
 match transport destination-port
 match ip protocol
 match interface input
 collect ipv4 dscp
 collect counter bytes long
 collect counter packets long
 collect timestamp sys-uptime first
 collect timestamp sys-uptime last
!
flow exporter FNF-EXPORTER
 destination 10.99.0.12 vrf DMZ
 source Loopback99
 transport udp 2055
 export-protocol netflow-v9
 template data timeout 30
!
flow monitor FNF-MONITOR
 record FNF-RECORD
 exporter FNF-EXPORTER
 cache timeout active 60
 cache timeout inactive 15
!
interface GigabitEthernet1
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input
interface GigabitEthernet2
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input
interface GigabitEthernet3
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input
interface Tunnel0
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input

Loopback99 here is 10.99.250.251 — Akvorado will SNMP-poll that address, which LibreNMS already proves works. Note template data timeout 30 is baked in from the start this time; you've earned that line.

Verify: run some inter-site traffic, then on the box: 

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/v0/outlet/metrics | grep netflow_packets_total
A second exporter="::ffff:10.99.250.251" series appearing = PBR-B is in.

docs.title: Part B — Q-EDGE (IOS)
docs.text:
Same FNF stack; the only differences are the interfaces and the export path (Q-EDGE reaches the NMS via VRF DMZ):

flow record FNF-RECORD
 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address
 match transport source-port
 match transport destination-port
 match ip protocol
 match interface input
 collect counter bytes long
 collect counter packets long
 collect timestamp sys-uptime first
 collect timestamp sys-uptime last
!
flow exporter FNF-EXPORTER
 destination 10.99.0.12 vrf DMZ
 source GigabitEthernet0/2.99
 transport udp 2055
 export-protocol netflow-v9
 template data timeout 30
!
flow monitor FNF-MONITOR
 record FNF-RECORD
 exporter FNF-EXPORTER
 cache timeout active 60
 cache timeout inactive 15
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input
interface GigabitEthernet0/3.98
 ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input

(Optionally add Gi0/0 and Gi0/4 for the DMZ side — then you get the pleasingly recursive sight of the SNMP polling and NetFlow export traffic showing up as flows.)

Two Q-EDGE-specific notes: - Source address = metadata gate. Flows source from Gi0/2.99 (10.99.2.1). If Q-EDGE's flows later drop with metadata missing, it means Akvorado's SNMP poll to 10.99.2.1 failed — switch the exporter source to whichever address LibreNMS polls Q-EDGE on, and it will pass. - IOL caveat: FNF on IOL is software-only and usually exports fine, but some builds are flaky. If show flow exporter FNF-EXPORTER statistics shows packets sent but nothing reaches tcpdump on the collector, that's the image, not your config — the cache still proves classification, and the exam doesn't care which box exported.

docs.title: Part C — the firewalls (multi-vendor flavour)
docs.text: This is the part that makes the estate feel real — and both devices must pass both gates: flow export and SNMP with REMOVED answering on the address they source flows from. Menu paths below drift slightly between versions; the verification loop at the end of this part is the ground truth.

docs.title: C.1 Palo Alto (PA-VM)
docs.text:
1. NetFlow profile: Device → Server Profiles → NetFlow → Add. Name AKVORADO, template refresh 30 sec / 20 packets, collector 10.99.0.12 port 2055. Leave "PAN-OS Field Types" unticked — enterprise fields just add noise to a standard decoder.
  2. Attach to interfaces: Network → Interfaces → each dataplane ethernet you want observed → NetFlow Profile: AKVORADO. Commit.
  3. Export path: PAN-OS sends NetFlow via its service route, which defaults to the MGT interface — confirm MGT can reach 10.99.0.12, or repoint it under Device → Setup → Services → Service Route Configuration → Netflow.
  4. SNMP (the metadata gate): Device → Setup → Operations → SNMP Setup → v2c, community REMOVED. Ensure the interface serving SNMP permits it (MGT does by default).

docs.title: C.2 OPNsense
docs.text:
1. Export: Reporting → NetFlow. Listening interfaces: LAN + WAN (whatever you want observed), version v9, Destinations: 10.99.0.12:2055. Apply.
  2. SNMP (the metadata gate): System → Firmware → Plugins → install os-net-snmp; then Services → Net-SNMP → community REMOVED, enable.

docs.title: C.3 Verify each firewall the same way
docs.text:
sudo tcpdump -ni ens4 udp port 2055 and host <firewall-flow-source-ip> -c 3
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/v0/outlet/metrics | grep -E 'netflow_packets_total|flows_errors_total'

Reading the errors counter is the whole diagnostic: metadata missing climbing for that exporter = fix SNMP / source address; sampling rate missing = shouldn't happen (the ::/0 default covers it) but would mean the default got lost from outlet.yaml; nothing climbing at all = the export never left (service route / listening interface).

docs.title: Part D — Akvorado touch-ups and the payoff
docs.text:
1. Name the remaining prefixes — add to clickhouse: networks: in ~/akvorado/config/akvorado.yaml: 

    192.168.0.0/16:
      name: lab-p2p
      role: transit
    172.16.0.0/12:
      name: gre-tunnels
      role: transit
Apply: docker compose restart akvorado-orchestrator akvorado-outlet akvorado-console

2. The verification cheat sheet (works for every part above): 

# who is exporting, and how much has landed:
docker compose exec clickhouse clickhouse-client -q \
  "SELECT ExporterName, ExporterAddress, count(*) AS flows FROM flows GROUP BY ExporterName, ExporterAddress"

# who is being dropped, and why:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/v0/outlet/metrics | grep flows_errors_total | grep -v '^#'

3. In the console: Visualize → set the dimension to Exporter → your whole estate in one sankey. Then dimension SrcNetName/DstNetName and watch gret-a-vlan20 talk to belv-b-vlan20 by name. That view — per-site, per-network, per-exporter — is exactly what an MSP NOC dashboard looks like, running on flow data you built end to end.

docs.title: Part E — stretch goals (expectations set honestly)
E.1 NX-OS sFlow on CSW1 — an experiment, not a promise
docs.text:
Real Nexus 9000s do sFlow well; the 9000v's virtual data plane may accept this config and sample nothing — and discovering that is the lesson (same family as your TCAM/PBR finding). Akvorado's inlet already listens on 6343, and sFlow advertises its own sampling rate, so no collector changes needed: 

feature sflow
sflow agent-ip <CSW1 DMZ-reachable IP>
sflow collector-ip 10.99.0.12 vrf DMZ
sflow sampling-rate 128
sflow data-source interface ethernet 1/5
sflow data-source interface ethernet 1/6
Verify with show sflow statistics on the switch and tcpdump udp port 6343 on the collector. Datagrams = delightful surprise; zero = write "sFlow unsupported on 9000v data plane" in your notes and move on.

docs.title: E.2 IOS-XR on the CEs — the sampling lesson, completed
docs.text:
XR requires a sampler-map — and advertises the rate via v9 options sampler-table, which Akvorado's decoder reads natively. So where IOS-XE forced you to configure a default on the collector, XR does it properly on the wire. Worth doing just to see both halves: 

sampler-map SM-ALL
 random 1 out-of 1
!
flow exporter-map FEM-AKVORADO
 version v9
  options interface-table timeout 60
  options sampler-table timeout 60
  template data timeout 30
 !
 transport udp 2055
 source <interface that reaches 10.99.0.12>
 destination 10.99.0.12
!
flow monitor-map FMM-ALL
 record ipv4
 exporter FEM-AKVORADO
 cache timeout active 60
 cache timeout inactive 15
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
 flow ipv4 monitor FMM-ALL sampler SM-ALL ingress
Commit, then check show flow exporter-map FEM-AKVORADO and the collector. Caveats: pick the source/destination path off show route 10.99.0.12 (add vrf <name> on the destination line if the CE's management path is VRF'd), and XRv's software forwarding may or may not actually emit — treat like E.1.

docs.title: E.3 vEdge cflowd — parked deliberately
docs.text: SD-WAN flow export needs a centralised policy pushed from vSmart — a proper exercise in its own right, and conveniently v1.2-relevant. Save it for an SD-WAN policy session rather than bolting it on here.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Per router: no ip flow monitor FNF-MONITOR input on each interface, then no flow monitor / exporter / record (PBR-A: keep, it's your Phase 3 build). PA: remove the NetFlow profile from interfaces, commit. OPNsense: clear the destination. sFlow: no feature sflow. XR: no flow ipv4 monitor … per interface, then remove the maps, commit.

docs.title: What this adds to the story
docs.text: One collector, five-plus exporters, three operating systems and two firewall vendors, with per-site named networks — plus you can now explain sampled vs unsampled export, v9 templates, options tables, and exactly which two gates a collector applies before trusting a flow, because you hit every one of them and read the counters that proved it.
